div.head: SALE OF WORK AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: SALE OF WORK AT LATCHFORD.
The Examiner, Saturday December 7, 1907,

whispered, there was not a soul who held out 9 warning hand or said, honestly: "You are on the brink of a precipice ! " "It was really scandalous ! " the gossips avowed: and yet—and yet, what is everybody's business it nobody's, for which reason not a saint or sinner adventured one kindly word or syllable of advice to lonely Kitty, who had never really loved her husband though he could easily have taught her gentle, sympathetic heart to adore him. And he, Sir James Linder, who came of a good, honest stock, proud of the valour of their men, the virtue of their women?

Well, he did not see. Perhaps, in that crisis of his life, be did not care to see; certainly just then • he had no time to think of anyone save himself. It is true to-day as it was when first spoken that "those whom the gods intend to destroy they first • deprive of their senses," and ever since evil or good luck sent that haul of gold won at cards, when he cleared in one night many thousand francs, the baronet had been mad as a sane man can ever be.

He went on winning night after night till he believed Fortune meant ..to stay with him for ever. He had the wildest dreams—all the wilder because he said nothing about them to any person. He Would pay off all the mortgages on the Warwick- shire property, which were eating the life out of the estate; he would renovate the town house; he would entertain royally. Kitty should know what a great thing it was to be wife to one of the Linders—dear Kitty, who had often chidden him for some slight extravagance, which chiding seemed trying to a man inclined to deny himself nothing. Perhaps it was for this reason, or perhaps because be knew he had been spending a good deal more than he had any right to do, that he said nothing to Kitty about those hundreds of pounds and the many, many hundreds that followed after. And she did not speak either. Since that morning when his dressing-room floor seemed carpeted with gold, and she had realised his was the sleep of a drunkard, a repulsion came over her, she grew strangely reserved. No longer did she wear her heart outside for all the world to see; for there was creeping in a secret she would have felt ashamed to reveal even to herself, and Jim's con- duct naturally fanned the flame. Yes, the poor young thing was falling—had fallen—in love with her brother's friend—the man who comported himself like a brother to the neglected wife. No tender word had he uttered, no single caress had he ventured, but the very tone of his voice thrilled Kitty, the mere touch of his hand seemed to be an assurance of sympathy and strength. And still Sir James, whom the gods—assisted by their obe.dient..quiritsi chatunturne and brandy.—were

he found she was natUrarehrotafit to make any promise such as he required, slapped her face and declared he would at once take her back to England to her scheming mother, Mrs. Thomas, 'whose reception she knew would be anything but cordial. "He told me to be ready to start to-morrow, and I know he meant it. And, oh, what shall I do? What am I to do ? "

"Come to me, darling, to me who loves you better than life. I will guard you, shield you, stand between you and trouble," and so on, to an accompaniment of passionate kisses, which, strange) as it may sound, were neither selfish nor dis- respectful. All the chivalry in the man's nature was aroused by the sight of her bitter distress. He did nob. stop to consider. He felt he would hive died cheerfully had it been possible for his death to make her happy. The poor little desolate, neglected wife, married to ,a gambler and a drunkard! The tender young thing who had hitherto borne her burden in silende. Ah, it was out of the fulness and pity of his heart that he poured forth those words of affection he had so Long refrained from uttering. . _ _ _

Eike a tired child she hid her bruised face on his breast. The weary little creature found comfort at last in his strength, and in answer to his pleading said: "Yes, take me away from this dreadful place. I cannot bear it longer. Take me away. When shall we go, to-night ? " He would have liked to take her then and there, as lie murmured soft words of love to the poor little, hurt soul, but it was needful for him to see to several matters, to arrange many things. They ought to be long leagues distant from Pau before Sir Janus returned to dinner; therefore at last he reluctantly tore himself away and went, as he said, to arrange matters, but in reality out in the street to face the difficulty that had so unexpectedly arisen, to realise that he was skating on the outside edge of propriety. Away from Kitty he no longer felt elated with his:success ; quite the contrary. He avoided the haunts where they had. been so innocently happy together, while a bitter regret intruded in his plans that he could not live through the morning again with a cooler head and a more bridled tongue. Ah, yes, he knew now what he had dote. He knew he had proposed a project that would ruin a woman's life. They might marry in the future, they might compass some sort of happiness, but the stain would remain—a blot on the white inno- cence of poor Kitty's once pure soul! Yet he had gone too far to retreat. He was bound in honour to proceed. Bound in honour? Yes, to take the woman's hand and go with. her to perdition! A great horror .fell upon him as'he- returned to

her back on the officer she bad learnt to love, anu hoping that in her mother-in-law's home she might become reconciled to the man who claimed her as his wife, the mother to be of his child. She was ready now to tread the path of duty, to find happi- ness in right. She had slept for some time, when there arose a strange stir and bustle in the hotel which could not possibly concern her. Then there ensued silence.

-Had she done wrong and gone off with Captain Fitzgerald, she would then have been fleeing through the night from conscience; as it was, though well- nigh broken-hearted, she could turn and go to sleep again. She rose early and dressed herself for the long journey. Looking forward to the peaceful rest awaiting her at the Dowager Lady Linder's, her heart aching for the sympathy she knew she was certain to find there, she slipped a note under her husband's door, and then, going softly down- stairs, begged the porter to fetch her bag as she wished to catch the early train. "But madame," he stammered. "Yes," she answered, strong in her integrity. "Evidently madame does not realise what has happened." "What has happened ? " "Sir Linder-"

"Yes, my husband ? " "Lost money—shot himself last night in the—" She dropped at his feet like one dead. They had parted in anger, but, God be praised, oh, God be praised, she had not left him. She had heard a voice from Heaven and listened to it, and she could kiss his poor pale face and weep and say: "My poor, unfortunate Jim 1" without hypocrisy. She could feel it was best for Jim to go, best for her to live for years and years most meagrely while the encumbered estate recovered itself; to sacrifice her life to her boy, born a few weeks after his father's death, and in his young life she found a new joy—she lived again in her child.

Never after that sorrowful day when she and "Jim " quarrelled; did she and Captain Fitzgerald meet again. He died abroad, leading a forlorn hope to victory, and left a pathetic little will which ran: I leave all of which I die possessed to Dame Katherine Linder as a token of my profound respect." Those two last words brought balm to her soul, as daily she thanked Heaven she had never lost her own self respect. She lived, a gracious British matron to whom no one in trouble ever appealed in vain, a lovely sad-faced woman whose eyes were full of the trouble of a long ago past, and whose own happiness centred round hrr son.
Women have been brave at all times. But not many women dare stab themselves and ary •" Pats

laglirig V& ruin, held on his wan career, rinking heavily to drown thought, gambling recklessly; more and more recklessly as his luck began to change, and he lost steadily night after night, raising as much money as he was able, borrowing where and from whom he could on the desperate chance of retrieving his position ' • for fickle Fortune, having wearied of the man she once smiled on, was now hounding him to destruction. . . _ _

Captain Fitzger-ald knew all that was happening, of course. Everyone in Pau knew exeept Kitty, and there was no use in telling her. Sir James had borrowed five hundred pounds from his wife's friend, and tried to negotiate another loan without
SUCCCSS.

Then the baronet., almost at the end of his tether, waxed exceeding wrath, and listened with ears On fire to gossip which a chance acquaintance "deemed it his duty" to repeat. Calling next morning somewhat earlier than usual, Captain Fitzgerald felt amazed and shocked to find pretty Kitty crying her eyes out. There was a nasty mark on her left cheek. She could not speak for gasping sobs ; she wept as though the bitter waters of her soul had burst their bounds. She only answered his inquiries with an hysterical "Oh ! Oh ! Oh!" and, hiding her pretty bead once again in the sofa cushion, wept such tears as he had never seen a woman shed before.

He took her hand, which she withdrew and put under her face. Then he began to understand and sat silent for awhile, scarcely knowing what to do. It was not long, however, before the fact of his presence began to exercise a quieting influence upon the little woman; bitter tears flowed less abundantly, gasping sobs were heard less frequently. "Can you not tell me ? " he asked at last..

But ;he only shook her head, and again he waited patiently. Suddenly, like a mountain torrent breaking bounds, she burst out: "0 Jim, how could you—how could you ? " "What trouble has Sir James been getting into now?" asked Captain Fitzgerald. "Tell me, and if I an help him I will."

Ent this kindly speech proved just the one thing too math. "You don't know—you don't know ! " she cried, with all the floodgates open. "He has been so unjust, so cruel. He has said such dreadful things ! " and she fell to crying again as if her heart would break.
Involuntarily Captain Fitzgerald's band stole to the fair soft cheek.

"What things, dearest? " he said. your friend." Then all in a rush the trouble was revealed. Savagely cross Sir James had that morning poured many vials of wrath on his wife's head, accused her of many sins, ordered her to hold no more rimumimicatinn with Carte Fitzgerald. a.nd whea

Ile would nave glven worms 10 reeni• the words he had spoken so unadvisedly; to be to Kitty again merely the friend he was before her husband's cruel blow, not a lover ;one to whom she could turn for advice and help instead of a com- panion in sin with whom she meant to flee. . _ _ _ . _

Aforetime be had faced death with a lighter heart than that with which he entered his xooms, often brightened during the course of many a perilously happy week by the memory of wistfully tender eyes and a sweet young face. The knowledge of what he was about to do made his strong spirit faint. In an hour or two -the past would be beyond everything—save regret. It was, even then, he felt as lie took up a note which lay on his table. It was from Kitty. No doubt to name the exact time she would be at the station. .Poor, poor Kitty! With reluctant fingers he tore open the envelope, grew out the enclosure, and read: —.tor-give me, please, tor dew, unable to do what I promised, but it would not right. I was in such trouble this morning I Could not think, or I should have known how terribly wrong all my deas were. I now intend to start for England early to-morrow morning alone, and go to my mother-in-law who has always been kind. Pray io not come to the station to see me off. I shall manage very, well. I cannot thank you enough foi 111 your gcodness which I shall never forget." A funny little fetter. Ah, what it had cost Kitty to write! Hours of battling with her inclinations rersus right, but, God be thanked, right had conquered.

div.head: PETER PAN IN LONDON.
div.p: PETER PAN IN LONDON.

ILondon theatres are looking forward to Christmas productions with great interest and the revival of Peter I Pan or the Boy who wouldn't grow up by J. H. Barrie for the fourth year at Charles Frohman's Duke of Yorks Theatre on Monday, December 16th is eagerly antici- pated. The value of the seats already taken and paid for amounts to some £6,000 or £7,000. Miss Pauline Chase will be Peter for the second season and Miss Hilda Trevelyan will play Vlienny as she has done in each production of Mr. Barrio's fantasy in London. Mr. A. E. Matthews will be Mr. Darling and Mr. Robb Harwood the Pirate Chief James Hook. The run of Peter Pan will last for some nine weeks in London, at, the conclusion of which period the company and pro- duction make their annual visit to a few of our big cities. Charles Frohman has arranged for Peter Pan (with Miss Pauline Chase and the London Comrany and production) to visit Liverpool for one week of nine performances in April next.

The memory of Dr. George Matheson is a cherished possession to all sections of the Church. With his sanctified %imagination and spiritual vision, he holds foremost rank among writers of devotional books. A happy idea has occurred to Miss Hatty Baker to make a collec- tion of his most beautiful prayers, assigning one to each day of the year. The little volume, under the title" Day unto Day," will be issued by the National Free Church Council in time for Christmas presentation. E. J. M.

div.head: FREE CHURCHES.
div.p: THE FREE CHURCHES.
(Prom Our London Correspondent.)
CHRISTMAS IN THE CHURCHES.

The month of December finds everybody in the midst of the season's work. Among the Churches "Socials," demonstrations and other meetings are being held night by night, and the wonderful machinery of the modem Church is working at full pressure. Christmastide means much to the Churches, and it might sometimes be asked whether we do not allow the oppor- tunities of the occasion to be captured too exclusively by those whose celebrations are in the very reverse of the Christian spirit. Some Churches, indeed, give up the whole of Christmas Day to the merry-maker, on the score of not being powerful enough to run a separate service. This difficulty is being over- come by Free Church Councils in many parts— a united service for the whole district being held, or, where this is impracticable, two or three Churches being grouped together. In this way not only is a successful gathering assured, but fresh illustration is given of the spirit of unity. Christmas is a time above all others when Christians should exhibit the spirit of brother- hood.

div.head: SUNDAY NATIONAL OBSERVANCE.
div.p: SUNDAY NATIONAL OBSERVANCE.

It is not often that Free Churchmen are present at meetings at Westminster Abbey— still less often is it when they come as repre- sentatives of the National Free Church Council officially invited. I was fortunate enough on a recent occasion to be present at a meeting held in the historic Jerusalem Chamber, Westminster Abbey. The Archbishop of Canterbury pre- sided, and on one side of him were Lord Avebury and the Rev. Thomas Law, and on the other Canon Ottley sat next to the Rev. J. Scott Lidgett ; facing them, Dr. Monro Gibson was sitting next Archdeacon Sinclair. It made one feel that the re-union of Christendom was a nearer event than had been anticipated. The object of the gathering was the promotion of National Sunday Observance. Representatives were present frcm some forty different societies, and the Conference unanimously passed a reso- lution recommending that a National Federa- tion or Alliance should be formed for Great Britain for the purpose of strengthening the existing Lord's Day Societies, co-ordinating their efforts, and taking action to promote better national observance of the Christian Sunday. The secretaries of the movement are Mr. R. P. C. Corfe, Rev. Thomas Law, and Rev. Canon Ottley, who have been requested to take practical steps to carry the 'resolution into effect.

div.head: FREE CHURCHMEN AT THE TREASURY.
div.p: FREE CHURCHMEN AT THE TREASURY.

I was also present at an occasion of a different sort, when some ten or twelve leading Free Churchmen waited on the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Home Secretary on the subject of next year's Licensing Bill. The deputation was headed by Dr. Rendel Harris, pretident of the National Free Church Council. Mr. Asquith humorously referred to the fact that whereas the congrega- tion usually outnumbered the minister, on this occasion the ministers had outnumbered the congregation. Ile assured thorn they were engaged in the familiar process of preaching to the converted, and the Government would do their best to make the forthcoming measure as effective as possible.

div.head: CHURCH MAGAZINES.
div.p: CHURCH MAGAZINES.

'The idea of a Church running a local maga- zine is becoming more and more popular,. and next year hundreds of Churches will be localising a magazine. Some weeks ago the National Free Church Council issued an advance copy of the January issue ot the _Free Churchman, whicn is specially produced for localising purposes. This number, with the programme for 1908, has met with extraordinary appreciation, and I learn that additional orders from all parts of the country are now being booked. Localisers say that it is the best magazine for localising pur- poses. It is possible that some Church secre- taries who are responsible 'for local magazines have not yet seen this issue of the _Free Cluirch- man. If so, I would strongly recommend thorn to write to the Publication Department of the National Council, Memorial Hall, E.C., for a specimen copy before they place their orders for 1908.

div.head: NEXT YEAR'S NATIONAL COUNCIL.
div.p: NEXT YEAR'S NATIONAL COUNCIL.

It seems early to be arranging for meetings to take place next March, but when they are on the scale of the great assembly of the Free Churches, the present month is not any too soon for planning. 1 have just received an advance proof of the programme of the National Free Church Council to be held March 2nd to sth at Southport. This preliminary programme certainly seems to promise a series of meetings of exceptional brightness. For instance, ser- mons are to be preached by Rev. J. T. Forbes, M.A., Rev. P. T. Forsyth, M.A., D.D., Dr. J. Rendel Harris, Rev. J. S. Simon, Rev. Alex. Connell, M.A., 8.D., Rev. W. J. Henderson, 8.A., Rev. J. D. Jones, M.A., 8.D., and Rev. J. H. Jowett, M.A. Other speakers on devo- tional topics are to include Rev. S. Chadwick, Rev. George Hanson, M.A., D.D., and Rev. John Thomas, M.A. Amongst the important subjects to be discussed I might mention two papers on "Christianity and Modern ,Economic Problems." The first of these is by Mr. Arthur Henderson, M.P. on "The Labour Movement" and the other on " Socialism " by Rev. J. E. Rattenbury. A -subject which should arouse ennsiderable interest, is being dealt with by Rev. J. Brierley, B.A. on "The Higher Criticism and Foreign Missions." The Rev. W. Bradfield, M.A., is to speak on "The Modern Passion for Pleasure." The Rev. C. Silvester Horne, MA., is to read a paper on "The Use of Money," whilst Dr. Horton deals with "The Corrosive Press." In addition to this we are promised the usual public questions, such as "Education," "Welsh Disestablish- ment," "Temperance," "The Congo," etc. The usual evening demonstrations will be held, and district meetings have been arranged on the closing Thursday night in some twenty neigh- bouring towns. The representation at these national assemblies grows more gigantic every year, and it may be fully expected that a record membership will be present when Dr. David Brook, the new President, opens the proceed- ings on March 2nd at Southport.

div.head: DR. HORTON'S DEVOTIONAL WORK
div.p: DR. HORTON'S DEVOTIONAL WORK

Dr. Horton in " The Open Secret "—perhaps the most popular of his books—suggested a method for the devotional reading of the Holy Scriptures. In order to further help those in- terested Dr. Horton has treated the Gospel of St. Matthew according to the methods he then tecornmended, and the result is a volume entitled "A Devotional Comnb•ntary on St. Matthew," which the National Free Church Council announce for publication in a few ,days.

div.head: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
Hare About Brook Pollution.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis— trict Council was held at Besysey Chambers on Wednes- day afternoon under the presidency of Dr. Murray. There were also present :—Messrs. J. Ball, G. Mather, W. Furness, A. Brooks, P. Longton, W. Houghton, Wm. Stanier, J. Backhouse, F. Kerfoot (inspector of nuisances), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), and H. 11. Burnage (aiststant surveyor).

div.head: DANGER SIGNALS WANTED.
div.p: DANGER SIGNALS WANTED.

A letter was read from Mr. W. Fairclougb, clerk to the Burtonwood Parish Council, asking if anything had been done in the matter of erecting danger signals in Burtonwood for the regulation of the speed of motors ecc. He was also to inform the Council that it was the wish of the inhabitants of Collins Green to have their houses numbered. There were 112 houses, and he requested the Council to take the necessary steps to have the work done.

The SURVEYOR said that when the first matter SVRa previously before the Council he explained that the erection of danger boards was in the hands of the County Council, and suggested that notice boards should be provided. Those boards were now on order. With regard to the numbering of houses at Collins Green, it would be an easy matter to have the work done if the Council desired it.

Mr. MATHER asked if the property-owners were not liable for the numbering of the houses. The INSPECTOR said it 'was the duty of the Council to do the work. It would not cost a sovereign and they had numbered houses at Sankey. It was decided that the work be done. TYE PROPOSED ALKALI WORKS INSPECTOR. _ _

Mr. A. BROOKS gave a report eil—t-ie-C;nfei-e-nCe held at Liverpool to consider thA appointment of an addi- tional Inspector of Alkali works for the Widnes and Runcorn area. He said the case for the surrounding rural districts was very ably put by Mr. Mercer, of the Whiston Rural District Council, who might almost have taken his brief from Mr. Backhouse, for some of his expressions were practically identical with those used by Mr. Backhouse at their previous meeting. The Warrington representatives did 'not think it was necessary to say anything further, except that they drew attention to the fact that the Government should pay one half the cost of the Inspector whereas up to the present they had only paid a third. They asked that the Government should be pressed to increaso their contribution. The result of the meeting was the appointment of a Committee of three to deal with the matter, and he thought the Council might be satisfied that in the hinds of those gentlemen the best would be done for all the districts concerned.

Mr. LONGTON : Will it be done quickly? Mr. BROOKS: When you have a Government department to deal with you have to hasten slowly very often, but I feel satisfied that the committee will do all they can to bring things to a satisfactory pass -- and that as early as possible.

div.head: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that during the month there had been 16 births and 15 deaths. The death rate from all causes was equal to 146 per 1,000 against 19°6 the average of the last three months and 21, the corresponding month of last year. Eleven deaths occurred in the County Asylum, Winwick. The proper death rate for the district was equal to 3.9 per 1,000 of the population. During the month one case of diphtheria and one case of erysipelas had been notified.

div.head: BROOK POLLUTION.
div.p: BROOK POLLUTION.

The INSPECTOR reported that in accordance with instructions Mill Brook, Winwick, had been inspected by Mr. W. Furness, Mr. Peter Longton, the Surveyor and himself and found to be badly polluted with sewage from the County Asylum. The brook was in a very bad state generally. Mr. LONGTON said the brook had been in that condi- tion for a long time. lie suggested that the Asylum authorities be asked to clean it out.

Mr. MATHER : Would you not suggest that they be stopped from turning in sewage in its present state? thought they had filtering beds. Mr. FURNESS said the deputation was fairly well satisfied that the Asylum authorities were not doing their duty by any means and he suggested that they be written to calling attention to their neglect in dealing with the effluent properly. They should further be given to understand that if there was no improvement proceedings would be taken. The Council ought not to be quiet and let things go on without protest. Mr. HOUGIITON : Do you think their system is efficient if it were attended to.

Mr. FURNESS : I think it is efficient if the cleaning out were done properly. Mr. LONGTON differed with Mr. Furness on that point. Mr. FURNESS said they allowed the brook to go too long without attention.
.. Mr. BALL: Hare they been notified before? The INSPECTOR : Yes. The Clerk has written them on the matter.

The SURVEYOR said that when the matter was before the Council in July he reported that the brook was polluted mainly by the effluent from the Asylum sewage works which in the opinion of the Medical Offioer, Inspector and himself were defective. If the alterations recommended were made they saw no reason why the effluent should not be clear. When the Asylum Medical Officer was written to he replied that a Committee had been appointed to deal with the question. It was decided to write asking how far the Committee had proceeded in the question.

div.head: MORE LIGHT WANTED.
div.p: MORE LIGHT WANTED.

The SURVEYOR read a petition signed by inbabitants of Orford calling attention to the "unfair distribution of light" by gas lamps from the tram terminus at Longford to Clambrook Bridge. A distance of 300 yards was lighted by only one lamp and the remainder of the lamps were something like 150 to 160 yards apart. The petitioners entered a protest against tbe unfair distinction as compared with the distances of other lamps toward Winwick. The CHAIRMAN said the road in question was a , straight length and be did not see the necessity for an I alteration.
It was deeded to reply stating that the matter would be considered.
A BURTONWOOD COMPLAINT.

The Surveyor said he had received a letter from the Bartonyood Parish Council protesting apinst the waste caused by the needless removal of materials, &c. He- was always getting something from Burtonwood Parish Council but they never gave any grounds for examina- tion of the complaint. In the present case be had replied asking for instances to be given. If there was anything of the kind complained of he wanted to get to the bottom of it.
It was decided- that the Surveyor should intimate that the Council required more definite information.

div.head: TRY THIS RECIPE for the simple Cure of NERVE AND BODILY, WEAKNESS. Costs a mere trifle
div.p: TRY THIS RECIPE for the simple Cure of NERVE AND BODILY, WEAKNESS. Costs a mere trifle

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Austrian Diamond .Inbilee.—The Emperor -Travers Joseph of Austria-Hungary, has this week celebrated his Diamond Jubilee. He ascended the throne on the 2nd December, 1843, so that he has reigned only 59 years, but it was decided to hold the ,celebration at the beginning of the sixteenth year, instead of, as in the case of Queen Victoria in 1897, After sixty completed vents of sovereignty. The Mmperor has only partially recovered from his recent severe illness, and there is still some anxiety concern- ing the state of his health. - His life has been full of vicissitudes, both as sovereign, and in private affairs, and it is not surprising that he feels the weight of Veers. He has fought unsuccessful wars against Prance and Prussia, hut while one was enough to drive lil Was oieon TT exile, TT[. into exe. the Emneror of Austria has managed to get the better of his political 'worries. But these have been ineessant, and in private life many misfortunes have befallen the Emperor. His Wife—the Empress Elizabeth—was murdered by an Anarchist, his only son died a violent death by his own hand, and his brother the one time Emperor of Mexico Was captured and shot by his rebellions people. 'Honour for Miss Nightingale —Never was honour More fully merited than that which has been eaestowed by the Ring upon Miss Florence Nightingale. She is the first woman to receive the Order of Merit, which was instituted five years ago, as the highest tribute tbatcould be paid to distinguished personalities. It ' has come somewhat late in the day, for Miss 'Nightingale is now in bar eighty-eighth year, but it May be that this is not the first time that a signal !loner's has been offered to her, although she could not .!ia prevailed upon to accept it.. Miss Nightingale has long been a confirmed invalid, and her eyesight has failed her, but she still takes a great interest in the Work to which she has devoted her life. Her courage and devotion in the Crimea stirred tbe whole world, _taut even more important were the services she rendered permnnently elevating the nursing profession by initiating the organised nursing of the sick, by women of education. Tt is to he hoped that she may be spared a while longer to inspire us with her presence, as she nillat always inspire 'is by her example. The Nightingale Femilv.—Miss Nightingale's father wes William Shore. but he assumed the surname of Nightingale in 1815, when he succeeded to the family Property. This came from Mr. Peter Nightingale, who w, as one of the pioneers of the factory system, and ]ndustrial revolution of the eighteenth century. He Ivaas one of the manufacturers against whom Arkwright, the inventor of the spinning jenny.brought an action for infringement of patent rights in MG. They were near neighbours. and Lea Hurst, the home of the Nightin- gales, in Derbyshire. is only two miles from Crornford, are Arkwright set up his mill. Miss Nightineale's an, other, Franees. was the danehter of Mr. William Smith, who for fifty years represented Norwich in Parliament, and took wee-. with Wilberforce in the great "nanti-slavery agitation. The Crimean heraine was born Florence, hence her name, and her sister, Lady °r °FT, was born at Naples, the two sisters being ior many years insenarable. The Barmaid Bnainess.—The question of the employ- -anent of barmaids is one of primary interest to those _engaged in that business, but it also concerns the whole army of women workers. There are said to he approxi- -ThatelY 100,030 women employed as barmaids and it is !Making that if they are to be turned 'adrift, it must, !end to greater competition and lower wages in other trades open to woman workers. It may be that no one even amongst extreme social reformers, ever centem- , Dieted taking such a cause, or doing more that prohibit- flew hands from entering this employment in future. ither way it would have the result eventually of foro- - Pgniany thousands of wemen into other trades, and it iS therefore satisfactory that Mr. Gladstone has givPn aan assurance that the Gevernment are not contemplating fly drastic meisarag of interference with the Pt:1100V- Zent of barmaids. • It is not an ideal occupatiOn for i"omen, and may present more moral dangers than some l.)thars, hut it would be out of place to abolish barmaids Y legislative enactment, whilst allowing women and girls to earn their living on the stage or as waitresses, or in other occnnations to which ol jections could also be found. No drastic measures are intended, but it is cleite that ROMA attempt. is to be made to impose safe- Walvis and limited restrictions upon the employment of barmaids, and to this end increased discretionary powers -will probably he vested in the Licensing Justices.. Christmas Gifts.—A delightful change has come over the spirit of present giving., which is something to be 'thankful for, as even a girl's consumption of photograph frames and cheap silver which doubles up when one -ventures to clean it, cannot go on indefinitely. Useful gifts are the order of the day, and no girl or woman is offended at receiving blouses, gloees, underskirts, dress lengths, etc.. etc. A choic tato in which we can never go wrong is handkerchiefs. A dozen, half-a-dozen, or even three dainty handkerchiefs are always appreciated by the well-endowed and impecunious alike, and the correct way to present them is net in a box, bnt in a sachet. And the latest sachet is built of pale-hued silk or satin, artistically painted with buds and butterflies. This is softly wadded, and bas about it a slight and elusive nerfume. The Passing of the Hich Heel.—No woman who aspires to be considered well dressed, will wear high heels, ont of doors, the heel of the moment being not More than an inch and a quarter in depth. and sloping slightly ferivard from the back. We ought to hear con- siderably less of aching backs and jarred nerves, both complaints no doubt, having frequently been brought on by walking—or rather attempting to walk—in high heeled bents or shoes. At the Jewellers.--Just now emeralds are in great ...demand, and the sapphire is retiring into the background somewhat: The great drawback to the latter beautiful Rem is its inability to "light-up "at night, even though surrounded by diamonds. The ancient world knew well the beauty of the emerald which seems to have first been discovered in Egypt and a'yria, and that it was Prized by the Pharoahs we know, by the specimens -which have been found on the Royal mummies. According to the American Indians. the emerald was originally a firefly, one of a swarm, which alighted on the earth, and was chanced into a gem. The stone is several times mentioned in scripture, and' it figures again and again in Arthurian legends, surrounded by an atmosphere of mystery and romance very fascinating to Minds wearied by the herd realism of latter day litera- ture. Lessons in Deportment.—lt would have been well indeed if all those among us who are responsible for 'the up-bringing and training of girls could have wit- 'messed the mingled dignity and grace of the foreign

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

LECTURE.—Last Friday evening the Vicar, Rev. J. R. Jones, gave a most interesting lecture in the Church Mission, the subject being, "The Qnest of life." The lecturer illustrated his subject with some splendid limelight views. Suitable hymns were thrown on the screen and the audience joined in them heartily. The operators of the lantern were Mr. James Woodward and Mr. G. Bates.

BIBLE Crass Socritt.—On Saturday evening the Wesleyan Men's Bible Class held a social in the day school commencing at 7.45. The President, Mr. C. E. Parker took the chair and a splendid progamrne was proceeded with, Mrs. C.E. Parker opening with a piano- forte solo, followed by a recitation," Our Folks," Miss B. Forshaw ; solo, Mr. H. Plumpton ; violin, Miss G. Henshall ; solo, Miss Balshaw ; solo, Miss Genie Bell. Mr. G. W. Weaver was the accompanist. The secretary, Mr. J. J. Foden read the reporf of ,the year, and remarked that the class had been able to supply the. Sunday school with several teachers during the past year, also that they had been ably assisted at the Sunday meetings by friends from Warrington and Widnes. Speeches were delivered by Mr. William Walker and Mr. W. Moores, members of the class. The Rev., J. F. Matthews, also addresed the gathering. Refreshments were then served by the members and their wives, after which games were indulged in until a late hour, and were much enjoyed. The committee who so ably carried out. the arrange- ments consisted of Messrs. J. Foden, E. Ashton, R. Long, R. Aideroft, T. Bell, J. Waine. W. Hughes, W. Balshaw, W. Walker, and A. T. Clay. The Rev. E. J. Gawne presided over the games.

div.head: AGAINST CONIPIILSORY SERVICE.
div.p: AGAINST CONIPIILSORY SERVICE.

At a meeting of the Clapham League of Young Liberals held on Wednesday it was resolved that the adoption of a system of compulsory general military training, as advocated by the National Service League, would not be for the welfare of this country.

div.p: ladies who have lately been visiting our shores. Deportment is the last thing we dream of teaching our girls, to their vety serious social loss, also to the detri- ment of their health, for contracted chest and stooping are hindrances to due development of lung and muscle. , The four daughters of the Comtesse de Paris are certainly among the finest examples we could possibly have, more especially the eldest—the Queen of Portugal and the youngest—Princess Lousie, the recent bride. The absolute ease and aplomb of these are in themselves a grace. Not a movement but is harmonious, yet apparently unstudied, inneed actually unstudied, for the study part af it is back in the past. in the gone-by schoolroom when girlish figures were held erect, shoulders flat, and heads were poised perfectly. Another Royal lady who personally superintended her daughters instruction in deportment is the Dowager Duchess of Saxe-Coburg Gotha. The Crown Princess of Roumania the Grand Duchess Cyril of Russia, the Hereditary Princess of Hob eplob e-Ln n genburg,and Princess Beatrice possess a regal carriage, and this is no doubt in great measure due to the rigid training which commenced so soon as they left babyhood behind. Long before they emerged from the school room, too, they were taught how to receive and entertaining the Dowager Duchess springing all kinds of situations upon them, so as to assure herself that they were ready in a gracious easy way for all emergencies. div.head: TEMPERANCE REFORM. INTERESTIU ADDRESS TO THE !JUNIOR LIBERALS. Disinterested Management.
div.p: TEMPERANCE REFORM. INTERESTIU ADDRESS TO THE !JUNIOR LIBERALS. Disinterested Management.

At the meeting of the Junior Liberal Association on Monday evening, Mr. J. Jamieson, of Manchester, who represents the Temperance Legislation League, gave an interesting address on" Temperance Reform." Mr. E. England presided over a good attendance. Mr. JAMIESON 68,id that for two years the Temperance Legislation League had been conducting a propaganda with the idea of educating public opinion on certain lines of reform which they felt were absolutely necessary at the present juncture' and particularly when they had a definite promise from the Prime Minister of legislation in the next Session of Parliament. As the result of the 1904 Act we were face to face for the first time in the history of the nation with a vested interest In licences, that we could not get rid of a licence, unless for misconduct on the part of the holder, without payment of compensation. Although the compensation was a levy on the trade, it was really a public fund with the sanction of Parliament. It was money raised by the public through the trade in order to pay off the licences not required. That was a very slow process. raking the suggestion of Lord Peel and his minority report that licences should be reduced to a limit of one to every 750 people in the towns and one to every 400 in the rural and urban districts, at the present rate of progress 73 years would elapse before a reduction to that extent was achieved. In order to effect that reduction, they would have to move the question of compensatiori out of the way as speedily as possible. The suggestion of the League was the enactment of a time limit to the operation of the compensation clauses of the Licensing Act of 1904. They would be glad to know that the Govern- ment was practically pledged to a time limit and that was certain to be one feature of the new Bill. That, however, would not carry us very far for the simple reason that there might be a recrudescence of the question in a generation, unless something was done to bring the whole licensing ques- tion under the control of the State. The League there- fore proposed that after the expiration of the time limit all licences should be regarded_ as new licences and be granted only on payment of the full monopoly value and for one year only. Even then the difficulties were not done with,beco,use once the State had recovered con- trol of the whole system, the State must also be able to impose the conditions on which the licence% were granted. As a matter of fact, prohibition was the law of the land and licensing was the exception. A licence conferred a monopoly but at the present time the holder did not pay the equivalent for that privilege. The League therefore asked that in future licences should only be granted on payment of the full mono- poly value. Whatever might be said about the 1904 Act, it actually introduced this principle, and the speaker gave instances of the greatly increased amounts which applicants for licences had had to pay in some localities. That principle should be extended to every licence, and in that way they would destroy the market value of licences, and it would not be possible to sell them at such exorbitant prices. While compensation was allowed, the League said the levies should he increased and also made compulsory and national, so as to get the full benefit of the Act. Then again the Act of 1904 .seriously tampered with the powers of local licensing authorities. When it came to a question of reducing licences the Benches, except in rounty Boroughs, bad no power. They simply had to report the places to Quarter Sessions, who had full power to dettrmine the question, and very often they were Mogether at variance with the local magistrates. The League therefore asked for the restoration and extension of the powers of the local licensing authorities so as to give them full discretion with regard to the grant or renewal of, licences and the imposition of conditions in connection therewith. Another important reform advocated by the League was that clubs should be brought under more definite control. The distribution of liquor in them should be declared to be a legal sale,and they should be required to contribute to the revenue. England was the only country in the world which granted preferential treatment to the clubs. The present system made it easy for people to do wrong, and- legislation must be directed towards the removal of the • bogus clubs which existed for drinking purposes only. Local authorities should also have power and facilities to enable them to establish and maintain counter attractions to the public-house in the form of alternative resorts where , full opportunity would be afforded for social inter- course and recreation, entirely apart from the sale of drink. It was a discredit to temperance people that this question had not been tackled sooner. Perks and recreation grounds were provided for the enjoyment of the people during the summer months but there was absolutely nothing to correspond to them in the winter. The League also maintained that power should he conferred upon localities within defined limits and under carefully considered conditions, to enable them, as soon as practicable, to promote sobriety in such ways as local conditions and public opinion might render • possible. This local option, or liberty of experiment, should : (a) authorise the Local Licensing Authorities to shorten the hours of sale on any or all days, and to require entire closing on Sundays and other special days. (b) enable a substantial majority of the people in a locality to prevent the issue there of ordinary gin palace, dram shop, and drinking bar licences, as dis- tinguished from special hotel and restaurant licences, and ordinary" off" licences. (c) Give power to place all the licences. or all the " on " licences, in a locality under disinterested (not municipal) management, in order that the traffic there might be conducted without the stimulus of private profit, and under statutory regulations which would prevent direct or appreciable pecuniary gain resulting therefrom to the locality itself. We had a very advanced Government in power with a huge majority, but there was not a majority in favour of entire Sunday closing. That meant that we were not likely to get entire Sunday closing under the next Bill, but if we could not have that there should be local option until the whole nation was ready to come up to that standard. Local veto, he maintained, was a democratic proposal. With regard to disintereeted management, he knew he was treading on dangerous ground. i Teetotallers were only one n ten of the electorate. I In order to carry local veto ia any looality, it meant that they bad to get besides the teetotallers, 67 out of every 90 men who drank to vote for the closing of a public-house, and that was the problem, which had to be faced. He had heard something about Warrington, and particularly about the recent municipal elections and what they did then, and if that was any indication he was afraid temperance sentiment was not very strong in in the town. Therefore, were they likely in Warrington to get 67 out of every 90 men who drank to vote for the ()losing of a public-house? The experience of other countries went to prove that they couli get local veto applied in the rural and urban districts, but that in the larger towns and cities they would not have it. The League therefore proposed that where they could not get local veto put into operation all the public-houses should be placed under disinterested management. The Bench, of course, would have the option of granting a licence to an ordinary

publican or to the company which would undertake the management in the interests of the community and not for private profit. Under disinterested management every grocer's licence would disappear, beoause by strict statutory regulation no house would be allowed to sell anything but the liquor itself. The company would have to provide all the money necessary for the experiment being carried on for three years: They would get the current rate of interest on their money and, by strict statutory regulation, not more than 1 per cent. The first charge on the profits would be the provision of a reserve fund equal in amount to the capital invested. That, reserve fund would in its turn be re-invested in Govern- ment securities to yield say 21 per centgand that would go towards the interest on the original capital, so that all the money that would go direct from the trade into the pockets of these men was at the most 1 per cent. All the profits remaining would go to die National Exchequer. Advantages of the system would be the , removal, as far as was possible under preseat circum- stances, of all pushing of sales for private profit, the elimination of the social element which would be pro- vided in the counter-attractive agencies, and the •dis- appearance of the tied house, and with it, the brewer's influence in politics. At present the trade was organizing its forces to such an extent that he believed that if, after introducing a Licensing Bill, the Govern- ment found it necessary to appeal to the country they would be defeated,because the trade was such a power in the land. They had only to change one vote on an average in every public house in the country from the Liberal side to the other side and they would turn the Govern- ment out and return another with s majority of 114. The question of the influence of the trade was worse than the House of Lords and th 3 League hoped to be able to deal with it on sane and reasonable lines. A short discussion followed.

Mr. J. R. GRIFFITHS said he was .in agreement with much that Mr. Jamieson had said,in fact the only point on which they really disagreed was that of disinterested management. He would like to know if Mr. Jamieson believed that under disinterested management the evil would be reduced. They were going to do away with the social element'and therefore the public-houses would exist amply for the purpose of supplying drink. If the company could not make sufficient out of the houses to build up the reserve fund and give their share- holders 5 per cent.,the scheme would be a failure. Did they believe the drink trade would be any the worse in the hands of a private individual, whose responsibility was on his own shoulders, than of a company who were simply grasping for 5 per cent? It had been proved already that the Public house Trust companies were as anxious to get their five per cent. as the ordinary publican who had to get his living. He agreed that the abolition of the grocer's licence would be a good thing, but could not they have that without disinterested management? He maintained that they could and that they ought to demand it. The demands were going up to the Government increasingly not only for the abolition of the grocer's licence and Sunday closing but for local veto as well. At the last election that was demanded and the Government was largely returned on those lines. They had had a majority of 223 in favour of local option and there was great reason to hope there would be a chance of bring- ing in a Local Option Bill w:thout the introduction of side issues such as disinterested management. The latter question, he contended, was not within the range of practical politics. He could not believe that a house in the hands of a private company would be any better than in the hands of a private individual. He would rather have one publican earning his living out of it than 10 or 15 men getting five par cent. He gave an instance of a Public House Trust actually introducing a public-house in a district against the wishes of the majority of the inhabitants. Mr. H. W. GUEST asked where the monopoly value paid by the licencees would go to and whether a licence°, losing his licence not through misconduct, would be entitled to the return of any of the money. ' Mr. JAMIESON said that Hr. Asquith had intimated that after Nfaach last all licensing fees would go direct to the National Hecheqner instead of te the municipali- ties, and therefore the monopoly valne would he treated in that way. Under the scheme as proposed by the League licences would be granted for a specific period, and when they were refused the publican would not be entitled to the return of any of the money. Mr. GUEST said that the more he heard of dis- interested management, the more he liked it as an alternative to leaving the matter entirely td local option. He often wondered how a place like Warring- ton would do with local option. He thought that if there was the option to increase as well as to reduce the licences, we would probably have twice as many public-houses. He moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Jamieson. Councillor HAWTHORN seconded, and said he was afraid they could not make people sober by legislation. There was no doubt that at the next general election they would feel the full force of the drink trade's influences. The sooner the closing of public houses on election days was enacted the better it would be for the temperance cause and progress. The CHAIRMIN was of the opinion that total abstain-6m should support any measnre of reform instead of always demanding the whole hog. The people were not prepared for local option. The vote was heartily accorded. Replying to the discussion, Mr. Jamieson Said he believed the elimination of the social element would nnquestionably reduce the drink evil. The experience of Norway and Sweden was distinctly in favour of dis- interested management. Four per cent. was the absolute limit of profit suggested by the League, not 5 per cent. With regard to the Pahlic Hens° Trust, the League was entirely opposed to it, while recognizing that it was an honest attempt to deal with the problem. The Trust, however, was in competition with the old system and therefore could not put its ideals into operaton. Not one Trust had made 5 per cent. and the promoters were working in the interasts of the public, as far as they could.

div.head: TW9 EX-MAVORS DEAD.
div.p: TW9 EX-MAVORS DEAD.
Alderman James Fairelough.

lir The people of Warrington heard with deep regret of the death of Alderman James Fairclough, J.l' , who I has passed away at his residence, Gatesgarth, Latch- ford, at twelve noon on Sunday.. For about a year he bad been in a delicate state of health, and it is a pathetic circumstance that his resigaatioe of the (Ale of alderman was to have been laid before the C )uncil on Tuesday evening. Last week it was seen that his condition was critical, but the news of his death came as a painful shock to the majority of the townspeople who had no idea that the end was so near. A useful public • career is thus brought to a close. Alderman Fairelou,,gli was the eldest son of the late Mr. James Fairalough, a gentleman who is still remembered by old Warring- toniang and was born at Billinge, near Wigan, in the year 1838 He received his education at Denbigh Grammar School and afterwards at Winwick Granimar School. His father commenced bueiness in 1832 at Billinge, afterwards building a warehouse at Earles- town, of which the late Mr. Joseph Evans,of flaydock,l was the architect. The deceased alderman was the senior partner of the well-known firm of Messrs. J. Fairclough and Sans, flour millers, Howley, who were the first (1873) to navigate the river Mersey by steam, the boat used being the Pioneer. They introduced the telephone into Warrington, and were the first firaa to order the automatic roller in Great Britain. Alderman Fairclough was a commissioner for Newton for about ten years. In the public life of Warrington he had long played a very active and conscientious part, ; bringing business acumen and a fearless outspoken- ness to bear in big work in the Council Chamber. ;He had served continuously as a member of the ; Council since the year 1891, being first elected for St. Austin's Ward. Afterwards he represented ; Latchford and St. Austin's Wards, and succeeded the late Alderman Charles John Holmes as an alder- man for the borough, in November 18913. There was a spirited contest over his election, the Liberals claiming that Councillor Henry Roberts who was the oldest Councillor, was entitled to the honour. How- ever, Mr. Fairclough was elected, by a majority of one vote. It was in 1891 that he was unanimously elected to the Mayoral chair and so well did he dis- charge the duties that he was twice re-elected in 1895 and 1893. Some words which he uttered in replying to a vote of thanks are characteristic of his blunt and outspoken way of putting things: —" I wish you could in your municipal elections do away with politics, because I believe yon are doing a lot of harm by intro- ducing them. When an election comes on you ga at it like' Kilkenny cats,' and create a lot of ill-feeling in the town. What have politics to do with the widening of a street, the enlarging of mains, the improvement and the cheapening of gas, and making ; the town healthy, sweet and clean ?" Alderman FairclonFh • took a •great interest in thel Gas Committee, of whiqh he had long been chairman, and he had also acted as chairman of the Finance and Estate Committee and deputy chairman of the Rivers ; Committee. A great honour was conferred upon him in 1897 when in celebration of the jubilee of the incorporation of the Borough he was elected an honorary freeman.; The only surviving freemen are Messrs. J. Charlton ; Parr and Frederick Monks, who were honoured in the ; same year. Alderman Fairclough was appointed a ; magistrate of the borough by the Chancellor of the Lancaster in 18N, and was very attentive to the duties. Alderman Fairclough was an enthusiastic sportsman It one time cricket was his favourite game and he did service for Newton-le-Willows. Warrington, and also for his county. It is intereeting to recall that he and Mr. John White represented Lancashire in their first county match. Mr. Fairclough was a golfer of great ability and had played in the matches England V. Scotland and England -v. Ireland. He also took an interest in billiards and could handle the cue skilfully. Amongst other appointments which Alderman Fairclough filled was that of trustee of the Blue Coat School. He was a staunch Conservative and a mem- bar of the Church of England. Alderman Fairclough's first wife was the eldest daughter of the late Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton Park, Newton-le-Willows. He afterwards married Miss Jefferson, his present wife who is the daughter of the late Mr. Thomas Jefferson, of Keswick, Cumberland. Much sympathy is felt with the widow and family (a son and a daughter) in their bereavement.

div.head: MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE.
div.p: MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday, the Mayor (who presided) made special reference to the death of Alderman Fairclough. He said it was his painful duty once more to announce the death of one of his brother magistrates. He must say it came to him as a very great surprise. He saw the flag flying at the Town Hall, but be did not know it was for their friend Ar. James Fairclough until he reached the Court. Their departed friend had been a member of that Bench for many of years, and had also filled the office of chief magistrates of the borongh. There was never a more conscientious magistrate and he administered justice tempered with mercy.He was a freeman of the borough— one of the highest distinctions his fellow townsmen could confer upon him. He (the Mayor) had to express the deep regret of the Bench with the widow and family of the late Mr. Fairo.lough in their sad bereavement. THE FUNERAL.

Striking testimony to the respect in which the late Alderman Fairclough was held by all sectiors of the community was afforded by the large attendance at the funeral which took place at Wargrave Church, NewLor, on Thursday afternoon. The members and officials of the Courkil and magistrates assembled at the Town Hall and proceeded to the late residence of the deceasel at Latchford where they joined the funeral cortege. At the head of the procession walked a detachment o: police under the direction of the Chief Constable (Mr. M.. Nicholls) and following them came a number o: employees of Messrs. James Fttirclough and Sons. div.head: Mr. R. W. Francomb J.P.
div.p: Mr. R. W. Francomb J.P.

Warrington has lost another esteemed public man by the death of Mr. Richard Walker Francomb, J.P., who passed- away at his residence, Victoria Pious°, Wilderspool, at 10.39 on Tuesday morning. For a long time he had been in a precarious state of health and recently he felt compelled to resign his seat on the Council and give up active public vvork. He had only been confined to the house for about a fortnight and his death while not being unexpected, created pro- found regret. Mr. Francomb possessed a kindly and genial disposition which gained him the respect and friendship of a large circle. He was always a ready and pleasant conversationalist and his commanding , figure was very familiar in the town. Mr. Francomb was the eldest son of the late Mr. Thomas Francomb, of Bristol, and was born on December Ist, 1845, at Newprt. He came to War- rington in April 1838 and was married on December 29th, 1869 to Miss Tolley, the only daughter of the late hir. William Jolley, of I.l.7arrington, who pre- deceased him on December 6th, 1905. Mr. Fran- comb's connection with the town's affairs began in November 1880 when he entered the Council as one of the representatives of the South East Ward. He succeeded at the poll,his opponents being Messrs.Ziba Armitage and Samuel Barlow; and he was continu- ously in the Council up to November of this year,never having been once defeated at a contest. He was elected an Alderman of the Borough on July 2nd,1889, succeeding the late Alderman John Pierpoint, and was Alderman of the Howley Ward. He did useful service on several important committees, and acted as Chair- man of the Water Committee. In 1886 he was appointed by the Crown a Justice of the Peace, and he was very regular in his attendance at the Police Court. On November 9, 1889, he was elected Mayor of Warrington, a position which he held for two years. He was very diligent in discharging the numerous 'duties of the office and earned the praise of the Council and of the ratepayers generally, It was during Mr. Francomb's mayoralty that the negotiations for the purchase of the water undertaking were brought to a successful issue. Mr. Francomb was the chairman of a small conimittee appointed to make terms, and after innumerable meetings and interviews, the bargain was completed. The alderman used to state that he was seldom ever away from the , Town Hall during the rrotracted negotiations. A , Bill was introduced into Parliament to enable the Corporation to take over the undertaking and to give legal sanction to the intricate and important terms of purchase. In the face of great difficulties, and in the teeth of the opposition of the Local Government Board ' the Bill was carried. Perhaps the most important provision obtained by the Bill was the suspension of the sinking fund for five Tears, and the compulsory redemption of the annuities, which brought about a great saving in the finances of the Borough. It was largely through Mr. Francornb's exertions that the Corporation undertook the erection of the public baths, and the foundation stone of the new building was laid by him on October 29th, 1891. In 1894 Ur. Francomb was elected to represent No. 3 division of Warrington on the Lancashire County Council, and he was an active member of the Finance and Parlia- mentary Committees. He also.represented the County Council as one of its members on the Asylum Board of Lancashire. He took a great interest in political matters, was an ardent Conservative, for many years deputy-chairman of the Censervative Association, and chairman of the Warrington district of the Newton Division Conservative Association. He also held the office of Chairman of the Conservative Club for a considerable time.
Much deep sympathy is felt with the family —two sons and a daughter —in their bereavement.
THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place at the Wart iugton Cemetery at noon, yesterday, and the large and representative gathering tested to the respect entertained for the deceased gentlenna, The members and officials of the Town Council met at the Town Hall at 10.30 and pro- ceeded to the late res; dance of the deceased at Wilders- nool, where they joir-.:3 the cortege. TOILET-MAKING IN COURT.

everal laundry girls who were witnesses in a ease at Marylebone County Court on Thursday caused amuse- ment by taking down and rearranging one another's hair, oblivious of the fact that in their elevated seats at the rear of the court they were in full view of Judge and jury.

Tbe author of the porten- THEODORE tonsly long letter to Con- ROOSEVELT. gress is the most interesting

American President since ABRAHAM LINCOLN. MT. ROOSEVELT, in fact, iusists on being interesting. He is himself interested in everything. His Presidenthl message digresses from Trusts to the breeding habits of birds, and from armaments to considera- tions about a National Gallery. In an ordinary man this would be m ore garrulity; but Presi- dent ROOSEVELT writes in such a manner as to compel attention. It was said of an eminent Member of our own House of Commons that he was a man with a strong style. Presi- dent ROOSEVELT is certainly the possessor of a strong style. Whether he is a strong man or a weak one must still be matter of speculation and private opinion, even though he has occupied the ' Presidential chair, and has expounded himself 1 through message after message, for a matter of seven years. In another year he will disappear into private life, and we shall probably not hear of him again. American Presidents are, with an exception here and there, like the bird in the Norse parable, which comes out of the darkness into a lighted room, flutters about for a while, and then once more passes into the darkness.

A man with so much freshneis of mind as Presi- dent ROOSEVELT may be relied upon to raise large problems. In a poen, by a countryman of his, RALPH WALDO EAERSON, there occurs a conversa- tion between a mountain and a squirrel. The mountain speaks in an appropriately large style about the great things that is able to do, and jeers at the Equiirel because it is only equal to the smaller tasks. "But neither," says the squirrels "can you crack a nut." President ROOSE- VELT is mountain and squirrel in one. He I deals with large things and small simultaue ously. What he leaves us in uncertainty about isaas to whether it matters. When he first went to the White House, and, in fact, before he went there, he told us that he meant to break up the Trusts; yet the Trusts have been growing stronger throughout the whole of the years during which he has been in office. There has been legislation about them, it is true. There have been convictions against some of them. Vast sums of money are to be paid in fines by the Standard Oil Company and other undertakings of that kind. But in the United States the law does not seem to get carried out where the possessors of millions are concerned. Mr. JOHN D. ROCKEFELLER has no more to fear, for the present at least, than Mr. HARRY THAW. By his attempt to deal with Trusts President ROOSEVELT has raised iaithe most colossal form the old question of whether it is proper or service- able for Governments to interfere with trade; but he has not yet supplied us with the answer. We can all see the evil of such a state of things as is depicted in the late FRANK NORRIS'S))OOk "The Octopus." A whole State is at the mercy of a single railway company, which can, and does, ruin all the corn :producers in it by flagrantly oppressive dealing. But what is the remedy for a condi- tion of things like that? Is it legis- lation against the oppressor ? Is it prosecution lin the courts? We should say in England that the destruction of the monopoly is the only possible remedy, and that the best way to destroy monopolies is to remove such legal safeguards as protect them against free competition. Trusts on the colossi scale can only exist in protected countries. Vast fortunes like those of Mr. CARNEGIE are less the result of business enterp ise than of protection from healthy competition. If any business concern in this country is found to be making more than 5 per cent, it at once has a competitor to meet with. But protection stifles all that healthy competition which is so necessary to the interest of the public at large. President ROOSEVELT stands by Protection. That is perhaps why his action against the Trusts has been so , ineffective.
THE LATE ALDERMEN FAIRCLOI7GH AND FRANCOMB.
The fact that three score years and ten is usually termed man's allotted span of life should prevent us being surprised or unduly

shocked when death calls some elderly public man away from the sphere of human activity to the life beyond. But this week the people of Warrington have had reason to be shocked in the death within a few days of each other of two gentlemen, both ex-Mayors of the Borough, end up to a month ago both Aldermen. Mr. James Fairclough had been in failing health for about a year, but few people anticipated that the end was ippt (aching so rapidiy. Mr. Fairclough rendered considerable service to the town as a member of the Corporation since 1891,and was one of five gentlemen who were Mayors of the Borough for three consecutive years. The others are Messrs. J. B. Pickmere, Joseph Harrison, Edward

div.p: Greenall and William BAton, of whom the latter is the only one now surviviog. Mr. Faircloagh made a very thoroughgolng and popular Mayor, hnd at no time of his life was his straightforward- ness of character more manifest than when he held this important office. Mr. R. W. Francomb only • reaigned his Aldermanic position a mouth ago, and up to the last fortnight he was about as usual though looking Anything but strong. His death came rather suddenly and following so closely upon that of his old colleague Mr. Fain:lough, created a painful sensation. Mr. Francoinb was the father of the Council up to the time of his retirement, having been elected in 1880. He gave valuable services to the town, and was Mayor - from 1889 to 1891.. Mr. Francomb had much to • do with the purchase of the:water undertaking and remained closely associated with that depart, meat throughout his membership of the Council. There is no doubt that the difficulties of the last few years in which the Water Commit-,ee became involved, told heavily on the strength of the deceased gentleman. It is remarkable how few members of the Council to-day are really entitled to the prefix "old." The mortality among the seniors of late years has been exceedingly high, and there is no doubt that the town is the poorer for the death ,of so many men of long business and , corporate exp erience.

--- The Progressive LAbOU THE GOVERNMENT League is n3t all9wing itr AND LABOUR, activities to diminish and the public meeting held in the Co-operative Hall on Wednesday evening, although not so large as it should have been, was a cause for congratulation. A more lucid and convincing statement of the biovernment'a work rt behalf of the work.ngclasses than that con- tained in the stirring speech of Mr. W. E. Harvey, M.P. for North Est Deebyshire, could nit have been desired. Mr. Hlrvey is one of those sturdy knights of labour who talk to workingtilen in a b. oniely,telling fashion which never fails to impress. He touched upon a variety of topics and showed that the Government is fulfilling its pledges to the electorate and has already done much for the cause of reform. Not the least illumlnating feature of his speech was his exalana:.ion of the disastrous effects to the coal trade, the workers and the ship-owners, of the notorious coal tax imposed by the late Government. The L:beral Government promptly redressed this real grievance with the result that the miners have regained the 10 per cent. which Was deducted from their wages, and the trade is happily in a most prosperous condition. Mr. Harvey rightly laid stress upon the GJvern- manes land legislation which bids fair to inaugur- ate a new era for the dwellers in the rural districts. Too long has landlordism exercised an unjust domination and impeded the nation's progress and all true reformers will rejoice that the Government is in earnest in tackling this all-important cries- ton ot the land-monopoly which lies at the root of all social amelioration.

Perhaps the central fact in COST OF THE any consideration of quiz's- Poos,-L.tw. Mous of the Poor-Law is the circumstance that 80 per cent.of the permanent indoor paupers are infirmary cases and persons of weak intellect. Ti4iB simplifies the great problem of the more satisfactory pro- vision for out-door cases and for old age. The -figures published in the thirty-sixth annual report of the Local Government B sard are striking enough, as showing the excessive cost—for such results—with which we are saddled by the Poor- -Law. Nearly half the total of £55,581,000 collectedl annually in rates goes to support the poor. Mere relief (apart from expenditure defrayed out of I loan) accounted for 14 millions. Per head of the population the outlay works out at 163. 61 in London and in the provinces at es: ; iii Denmark, where a system comp ira- tively ideal prevails, the cost is only 53. 81 The London indoor naupsr costs £36 65.; the outdoor £8 ls. 7td. Yet Mrs. S.llars declares in the "Nineteenth Century" this month that in Vienna workhouses the cost per head is but 101 a day, as compared with London's 23. 71 Indeed, in the most beautiful old•age homes it is no more than is. 5.1. Berlin can shew us how to do it for 91 However these figures may be discounted,the case f r reform is made out. Beyond the 80 per cent. of infirmary and asylum cases there is the need for either better and more modern provisions in this country or for more economical administra- tion.

There has been an earthquake every night this week in Warrington—at the Royal Court Theatre !If is terrifyingly real, and the bang when Claudian's palace collapses can be heard in Sankey-street. Passers-by at 10 p.m. have been seen to jump away from the theatre as if they were sh,t, or expected to be.

o They were celebrating a victory at the recent rauni- cipal election, and one guest, who had been very attentive to the free beer, began to complain that he had never before been paid for his vote. " But you had a hare last year," said one of the" workers." "It was full of maggots," was the retort. " Well, then," remarked another of the guests, "if it was not bribery it was corruption."—" Daily News." * *

Mr. James Tomkinson, M.P. for the Crewe Division, is making a tour of his constituency previous to going on a visit to India. Mr. Tomkinson was visiting , India at the time of the general election, and had to hurry back for his election. The hon. member is ' starting with his daughters on December 6th, and will not return until the middle of February. He has -paired for the opening of Parliament. * A. switch in time savcs a fine. —MtzsEn. Most true things are in bad taste.--41011S OLIVER HOBBES. A man has more fun f'r th' things he hasn't got thin injyin' th' things he has got.—" MR.DOOLEY." To see the direction in which humanity in travelling ought to be the purpose of every strong and healthy intellect.—HAMEßTON. A wife is Miss-appropriated. —PULITRER. Pleatant company always accepted. --MU3IFORD. 0 * Mr. Howes had his little joke on Wednesday with regard to the three wedding ceremonies which Mr, Crosfield, M.P., had gone through in Paris. "He has got married more than once, so I suppose, it is a perfect job" said Mr. Howes. "I was only married mce myself, and it has lasted right up to now." Obviously therefore, Mr. Crosfield's wedded life should be three times as long as that of Mr. Howes. We could wish him nothing better. Mr. Howes has only been married about 40 years!

* * * More " glorious news." The date of the departure I of the last Chinaman from South Africa is not very far distant. When that day arrives, Mr. llowes suggests that there should be a celebration in War- ' rington, participated in by Mr. R. L. Outhwaite. We cordially say" bear, hear "to this. Mr. Outhwaite's statement of the case against the randlords in that memorable meeting at Parr Hall is still fresh in the recollection of all who were present, ani to renew• acquaintance with the gentlemen who fought "Joe" entirely on the pig-tail principle would be a pleasure. * * * Much interest has been taken recently in the demolition of the old Pin Mill, Knutsford-rbad. Little now remains of the building but the tall chimney stack which seems' to stand menacingly over the road. Speculation has been rife as to the way the chimney' would be felled in such a confined space. We under- stand that Mr. Hewitt, the local steeplejack, is to under- take the task by underpining the structure and then burning out the pins so that the chimney will gradually collapse in a heap. This is what the chimney is expected to do, of course, but we should imagine that the houses opposite will he deserted while the operation is in progress

PUBLIC BENEFIT.—IIEDEK THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRL—Advt. Visit of a Famous Band. . Warrington people are looking flrward with great interest and pleasure to the visit of the famous band of the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment which takes place during the coming week. It will be remembered that the band came to Warrington on the occasion of the unveiling of the war memorial by General Buller and won great popularity. Since then they have been to France where they had a remarkable reception. Two concerts have been arranged. The first will be held in the Parr Hall on Thursday even- ing next at 8 o'clock and the second in the Hippodrome on the following Sunday afternoon at 3 o'clock. The proceeds are to be devoted to a very worthy object the Cottage Homes of the South Lancashire Regiment. On Friday evening next a Public Ball in aid of the Cottage Homes will be held in the Parr Hall. The string band of the 2nd South Lancashire Regiment will be in attendance. A parquet dancing floor will be laid specially for the occasion.

resolutions of protest have been adopted by local ; Councils and by public meetings in the districts served lby the Inspector, but without avail. An old Police ' Act (1839) gave this absolute power of dismissal to County Chief Constables. In cities and boroughs the supreme control is vested in Watch Committees, but 'no subsequent measure of self government has given the counties similar control over their police.

The appeal from General Green Wilkinson, Chair- man of the National Association for the employment of Reserve and Discharged Soldiers, on behalf of lex-soldiers seeking employment, cannot be made known too widely in view of the large number of such men i discharges from the colours returning home at this ;season of the year. The ex-soldier i&entitled to much icalsideration and sympathy from the public, and !amongst other employers of labour who have assisted tin the effort to procure work for ex-soldiers, it is noticed that the London and North-Western Railway Company have again done well, returns recently rendered showing that during the twelve months ' ending September last, 2,656 ex-soldiers were given employment, compared with 1,832 during the corres- ponding period in 1906, or an increase of 824 men. I This example should be emulated by employers of I lab...Lir generally, especially those municipal and 9ther cwporate bodies and departments which spend public ;moneys on the provision and maintenance of public works.

. _ 13 Facts are facts, of course, but much depends on the way they are dressed up. For instance, the " Observer" of last Saturday in announcing the Liberal victory at West Hull remarked "at the IGeneral Election the Liberal majority was 2,247, now ! reduced to 241." This must have been very comfort- ing to those Tory readers who swallow implicitly all ' that their party paper serves up for them. But if the election figures are carefully examined they will be found to have an entirely different significance, which we will take the trouble to point out to our Tory friends. In 1906, when the Liberal majority was 2,247, there were only two candidates, and it was the !Conservatives who were so far behind. Last Friday there was a third in the person of a Labour candidate, who polled only 800 votes less than the Conservative. Both Liberal and Labour were pledged to Free Trade and reform, so that the actual Progressive vote was 10,125 against 5,383 for the Conservative. The Pro- gressive vote increased by 1,483, and the Conserva- Itive vote fell away to the extent of 1,023. As a matter of fact the West Hull election was a great victory for the Liberal, a moral victory for Labour, and a hope- less defeat for the Conservative. Toryism and Tariff ! Reform were out of the running!
