The Infirmary. Dr. C. Richards m Brown, junior house surgeon at the Infirmary, has peen appointed senior house surgeon in succession to Dr. Alexander Hodgkinson, who is going into private praoice. Dr. G. H. H. Russell takes Dr. Brown's place as junior surgeon. Mr. H. Berrey's Musical Evening. The large audience which assembled in Cairo-street schools on Thursday on the occasion of the musical evening arranged by Mr. Harry Berrey, the talented conductor of the Apollo Prize Choir, enjoyed a programme of more than usual interest and variety. It was sustained almost entirely by Mr. Berrey's pupils and the way in which all acquitted themselves spoke volumes for their own capabilities and the excellent ins.:ruction which they receive at Mr. .Berrey's hands. The items were sufficiently diveisified to cater for all tastes. There were songs sentimental and religious, solos in Italian and French, beautiful duets and humorous quartettes. Some of the artistes had had comparatively small experience of public singing whilst others had evidently gained honours on the platform but all- did well and were rewarded with rounds of cordial applause. The artistes were : Misses Florence Bennett, Edith Maybury, Eleanor Slater, Emily Holmes, Jeannie Armstrong, Cissie Hankey, Gertrude Povey, Lily Fairhurst, Edith Chalmers, Maysie Thompson, and Alice Woodland, Madame Nellie Booth, Messrs. Ernest Walker,William Parker, TA. Vernon, Bert Plumpton, W. J. Booth, George Radcliffe, Arthur Greenough, and a quartette consisting of Messrs.Harper,Mayers,Eniery and Tickle. Mr.W.Pearce acted as accompanist. The proceeds of the concert will be devoted to the funds of the Apollo Prize Choir. Full details from the local agent.—J. S. GARLAND, 51-55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Crosfield Ambulance Team. At the annual ambulance contest at Nelson on Saturday, the above team obtained the second prize, nine teams competing. For the prizes given to the three competitors- scoring the highest aggregate of marks, three men tied, I. 0. Roberts and J. Nevrns of the Crosfield tearnbeing two of them. A further test, tracing the course of the arteries in the upper part of the body, resulted in a second tie. Subsequently a request to treat a fractured knee-cap and a thigh bone broken near the knee, resulted in Roberts scoring 16 marks, Newns 15 and the third man 10. As a further illustration of the severity of these competitions, the questions set are appended and it speaks volumes for the zeal with which this unselfish and important work is studied, that eight of the nine teams scored over. 75 per oent. of the maximum marks, the winning team, Crompton, attaining over 92 per cent. and Crosfield's comiug next with 90 per cent. The viva voce questions were :—(1) Describe the nervous system. (2) How would you proceed to examine a patient who is insensible? (3) Describe the respiratory system. (4) Describe burns and scalds and how would you treat them with and without assistance. (5) What is the state of the pupils, respira- tion and pulse in concussion, compression, apoplexy, collapse from drink, epilepsy and hysteria. The stretcher test was : —Fractured upper arm bone and compound fracture of the shin and fibula bones. The individual tests were : —(1) Fractured knee-cap, no regulation splints or bandages to be used. (2) Fractured ribs, patient coughing blood. (3) Bleeding left palm and fractured upper arm bones one inch above thik elbow joint, afterwards told patient fainting. (4) This man is insensible, and is lying with his right hand across an electric wire. (5) This man is found insensible in his bedroom, treat him. Buy HARRIS'S WILTSHIRE BACON at ASHLEY'S.—Advt. There was an attendance of over 239 at the annual tea and concert in connection with the Wycliffe Society which took place on Siturday and proved a great success. An excellent concert was given in the Memorial Hall,presided over by the President, the Rev. John Yonge. The following ladies and gentlemen contributed musical items, which were greatly enjoyed and appreciated by a large audience, namely, the Misses Farrar, Griffiths, Peacock and Beswick, and Messrs, J. Willett, William Rutter, and Pearce, and Master Lawton, the juvenile comedian, who created roars of laughter by his rendering of the character song " Killicrankie. ' On the proposition of Mr. Richard Atkinson, seconded by Mr, W. Crosskill, and supported by the Secretary, hearty votes of thanks were accorded to the ladies for providing the tea, to the entertainers, to the Rev. John Yonge for presiding, and to Mr. W. H. Payton for accompanying the artistes. —There was a good meeting of the Society on Sunday, presided over by the Secretary. Mr. Worthington, of Wigan, gave an address upon " Unrestfulness," He said be was daily; reminded of this. There was great dissatisfaction abroad, and he did not find fault with it, as he looked upon it as a healthy sign. When they were altogether satisfied there was danger. He -appealed fora spirit of improve- ment within; there were outward signs of improvement. Mr. G-reenough sang "My hope is in the everlasting" and " Deeper and deeper still," which was greatly appreciated. Mr. Haley and Mr. Cattoa also took part in the meeting. There are now 439 members. The singing of the hymn "Sound the battle cry "brought the meeting to ' a close.—An open meeting of the Buckley-street Society was held on Sunday afternoon, when there wis a large attendance of members and friends. Mr. James presided. The speaker was Miss Margaret Radcliffe, the missioner, who is conducting a fort- night's mission at the church. Miss L. Plinston (contralto) and Miss N. Woodland (soprano) were heard to great advantage in their solos. Miss N. Plinston was the accompanist. Messrs. W. Shaw and J. Knowles took part in the service. PUBLIC BENEFIT—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR Bist BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. LINSEED COMPOUND' for Coughs and Colds. Of proven efficacy. Of Chemists.—Advt. "In the Lana of the Brigands." On M nday evening a lecture on the above subject was given in the Co-operative Hall, Cairo-street, by Miss Fredlux. The lecture, which was illustrated by lantern views and native costumes; was descriptive of the Christian work in Macedonia, and the proceeds were to be devoted to thl International Mission School, Salonica.—Mrs. Robert Garnett presided over a small attendance.—Mrs. Garnett said she was very much I interested in the work in the East, as she had taken , some personal interest in schools and missions in both I Egypt and Palestine. —Miss Fredoux said nearly 100 I years ago her grandfather lived near Warrington, and one evening he walked into Warrington and saw a placard on Warrington Bridge. On the placard there was the notice of a missionary meeting. He had been converted amongst Wesleyan IMethodists, and the sight of this placard turned his attention to missions, and the result was that he became a missionary. It, therefore, seemed very 'fitting that she should give her first missionary lecture in Warrington under the presidency of Airs. Garnett, ! a Wesleyan Methodist. (Applause.) Miss Fredoux then proceeded to give a description of her work !in Salonica, which silo explained was the I Thessalonia of the Bible. She detailed terrible ! deeds of revenge practised by Greek against Bulgarian- t and Bulgarian against Greek, and also spoke of the I great difficulties under which missionary work was I carried on there. She gave some interssting accounts about the attempt to assassinate the Sultan by a bomb t explosion in Constantinople, of which she was an eye- witness. At the c3nclusion of the lecture some beautiful lantern views, most of them taken by Miss Fredoux, were thrown on the screen. On the motion of Mr. J. Marsh, seconded by Councillor Skelland, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mrs. Garnett for presiding.

Children's League of Pity. A meeting of this branch of the N.S.P.C.C. was held at the Win narleigh Cafe on Saturday afternoon. Miss Broadbent presided and she, was supported by Mrs. Frank Bush. There was a large attendance. Miss Broadbent said that since their last meeting they had lost one of their members, Miss Greening. She had only just joined the league of pity and she asked the other members to stand to show. their sympathy. A n address was given by Mrs. Bush in which she gave instances of how children were neglected and how the N.S.P.C.C. had saved them from what would have been death. So badly were some children treated that on being admitted to homes they did not even know how to get into bad. The society had 466 chil- dren in their care in various homes and 202 inspectors. After the address Miss Broadbent announced that nineteen new members had been enrolled that after- noon'and that Miss Dorothy Cox had brought five new members and she was therefore entitled to the "recruit's ribbon." A. RUGBY UNIONIST ON THE ALL BLACK." This month's issue of C. B. Fry's Magazine contains an interesting article on " The New Zealand Profes- sionals" which is unsigned but probably written by a Rugby Unionist. After detailing the origin of the tCur and the negotiations which led thereto, the writer makes the following observations on the pro- fessional "All Blacks."

"I do not see at all eye to eye with those critics who say that in the Bramley m itch the New Zealanders were beaten forward while packing two, three, and opposing six men by five and that they were "obliged" to send Tyler back into the scrum. This is not so, as for one thing, Tyler did not go back into the scrum until half way through the second act and of the twenty-five points scored by the visitors, seventeen were scored while they were packing two three with Tyler" roving."ln the Bromley mitch they were often beaten for possession, but that was more due to the lack of familiarity with the rules possessed by their half who put the ball in the scrum as well as to the " overhand," " bouncing down" methoi practised by the Bramley half-backs--a method never seen in the proper Rugby game —than to the two three shape being beaten by the. three two one."'

"Under Northern Rugby Football Union rules the ball must not be kicked direct into touch, except with a penalty kick. It must bounce first. The most ridiculous rule ever devised to spoil a' game, in my opinion. But there it is, and these men had to see glorious punts, that would have brought the house down in a proper game literally penalised, as a "serum 'r was formed whence the kicker had punted, although he had found touch fifty yards down the ground. The rule does not make the game faster, which it is popularly supposed to do and, moreover, it puts the baa kicker and the funk on a level with the good one and the plucked one. This is absurd. Cessations are constant when the ball, as in three out of five kicks it does, finds touch. Thus the players are frequently rested. And the coward when at all Cornered merely kicks —somewhere anywhere, so long as he kicks. Should- he have "chanced on a good one" (the best i the Northern Union game generally go straight to an opposing back, who returns the ball after a ran of five or six yards straight to another -player, and so it goes on until the ball drops into touch, when a scram is formed or someon6 is ruled off-side, as happens in 70 per cent. of the kicks) he comes in for wholly unmerited kudos. In the Bramley match there were quite twenty pints by Bramley players straight up into the air which were obviously of the "I must get out of this somehow" order, and each ended as the ball fell on a scramble that was neither Rugby,-Soccer, nor any Lam of football."

" The problem before the New Zealanders on this tour is to get full value out of their superb kicking ability and I do not see how they are going to do it in the face of this absurd rule —a rule which negatives the whole arts of obtaining position by punting and of turning defence into attack by means of long and accurately ganged touch finding."

"All Blacks" 1905 v. "Pros." 1907. —ln so far as it is possible on the evidence before me to form an opinion, I think that D. Gallaher's fifteen would beat the present fifteen giving the latter G. W. Smith, D. McGregor, W. Johnson, and W. Mackrell who were also under Gallaher."

"The present team has not a Roberts or a Hunter,a Gillett as a full back for kicking, a Sean(' Newton, or a Cunningham. H. H. Messenger may be as good as W. H. Wallace —he is unquestionably a finer place- kicker—and E. Wrigley may be as good as A. G. Deans but neither is a better player. The present backs as a body are slower than those of 1905, the forwards are not as a body such a fine set of men, though T. Cross of this team is as good as any of Gallaher's pack except Seeling. W. T. Wynyard is not I sheuld think, as good as Roberts as a half and certainly not as good as Hunter as a five-eighths. G. W. Smith is quite as fast .as he wa,sin 1905 and every bit as pod, but he was, perhaps, not the fastest back of that team, while he is unmistakeably the fastest of this."

" Professionalism as the present team proves, has ' taken definite shape in New Zealand, and it has sown the seed of rivalry in New South Wales by the defeats of last August. The Rugby Union thus finds profes- sionalism hydraheaded —Yorkshire, Lancashire, Cumberland, Cheshire, New Zealand, New South Wales, Victoria (for this team as ha been shown was invited to play at Melbourne) have all got their pro- fessionals. Tae stamp of player in New Zealand and Australia is just the one for professionalism. This professional movement will never kill the game— certainly not under Northern Union rules, which it will be something to wonder at if the New Zealanders adhere to after their tour—though it will rob it of of many of its most accomplished players in the Colonies."

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovalist."

Lancashire was fog-bound on Saturday, and great was the disappointment animg football enthusiasts, particularly at Warrington, where the important engagement with Wigan should have been fulfilled. All the morning people were discussing the prospects and hoping against hope that the fog would graciously clear away in time for the match to be playei. At noon there seemed an outside chance, but the ray of light which filtered through was only a sort of tantaliser. Thereafter the fog thickened steadily until at 3 o'clock it was only possible to see the width of a street,and that indistinctly. Nevertheless a few hundred hopeful enthusiasts wended their way to the ground. What they expected to find, I d m't know, unless they had some reason to anticipate a providential dispensa- tion in the shape of bright sunshine between goal-posts and touch-lines at Wilderspool. Faith is a wonderful thing, but the fog dispelled it on Saturday.

Most people felt sorry for the Club, as well as personally disappointed, for the postpoaement of such an important match might easily result in the loss of £lOO. Luckily both Clubs had an open date, and the match has been re-arranged for Saturday, February 22nd. This is the ueek fnllowing the Warringtoa match at Wigan and should gain in interest on that account.

The only match of any importance which was played in Lancashire on Saturday was at Rochdale where clear weather prevailed and the final for the Lancashire Cup was decided. The holders, Broughton Rangers, fancied their chance of retaining possession of the trophy, but undefeated Oldham proved too strong for them and won the Cup by a: fair. margin. Oldham seem to be making amends for missing both the League and N.U. Cups last season.. At present they look like carrying off the Lancashire and Northern League championships also, but they had better take warning from past history and not be too cock-sure. Oldham's success strikes nil as being somewhat remarkable for they are by no means the brilliant team of old. Solidity and soundness in all departments, coupled with determinatios, seem to be their winning assets this season. I am sorry they have already been to Warrington and snatched a victory. Had they come later there would be a chance of Wilderspool becoming their Waterloo.

The" All Blacks "have been showing something like their best form again this week. To beat Dewsbury and Batley combined by 18-8 on Saturday was very, satisfactory, and this performance was followed up by the swamping of Swinton in a sea of mud on Wednesday. In both games the New Zealanders gave evidence of having got back into condition, and were much too good for their opponents.

Interest in the Warrington match is increasing, and if the "All Blacks " maintain their form there should be a huge gate at Wilderspool on December 21st. A large nulnher of tickets have been issued at 2s. 6d. and 3s. 6d. for ground and stand, and enclosure and stand, respectively. Admission to the ground will be is. and is. 6d. Members will be admitted free and special seating accommodation at a charge of 6d. will be provided round the inside of the rails.

div.head: WARRINGTON PUBLICAN'S FAILURE.
div.p: WARRINGTON PUBLICAN'S FAILURE.

At the Warrington Bankruptcy Court, yesterday, before Mr. Registrar Ridgsa,ay, Frank James Whittle, late licence& of the Marquis of Granby Inn, Church- street, appeared for his public examination—Mr. F. G. Taylor (Messrs. Henry Greenall and Co.) represented petitioning creditors and Mr. T. S. Steel appeare:l for the debtor. In examination by Mr. Johnson (assistant official receiver), the debtor stated that he commenced business as a licensed victualler at the Marquis of Granby Inn, in September, 1901, with a capital of £2OO derived from a policy effected on the life of his late mother who had previously carried on the business since the death of his father on September 27th 1890. He paid £lO6 3s. 7d. for the stock &c. He also took over ' and paid his mother's debts which he estimated at £155. His failure was mainly due to insufficiency of the profits of the business for his maintenance and that of persons dependent upon him. He estimated that the profits for the three years he carried on the business amounted to about £lO4 and household and personal I expenditure totalled about £390. H 3 had incurred con-1 I siderable expense through illness in the family. He I could not say when his insolvency first arose but he thought it must have been more than a year ago. He I had had two loans from the Latchford Advance Office of I £5O each. In each case he gave a promissory note for I £62 payable at £5 a month. He borrowed £67 3s. from Mr. Charles Paikin and gave him a promissory note for ! £73 payable at £7 a month. The loan granted to him by Mr. Paikin was secured by a bill of sale on his household furniture and business effects. He borrowed the money to pay out two executions which had been levied on his goods. The furniture had been sold since I the receiving order had been made and had realized Isufficient to pay Mr. Paikin's claim in full. The only excuses he could offer for his failure to keep books of account sufficiently disclosing any business transactions and his financial position from time to time were that he kept the same kind of books that his late father had kept and that he did not know it was an offence in bankruptcy to omit to keep others—namely a cashbook and creditors' ledger. His unsecured. liabilities amounted I to £393 14s. Bd. aad his asset to £3O ss. 41., leaving a ideficiency of £3lB 9s. 4d. The examination was closed.

Readers of this column. are invited to assist in making it interesting and helpful to social workers by contributing themselves. Correspondents must write on one side of the paper only, and endeavour to make their letters and notes short and to the point. A nom-de-plume may be used, but the real name of the writer should be forwarded in confidence to the Editor of the column. 31.5.5. must be addressed to John Workman, " Examiner " Office, Warrington and should be sent in not later than Wednesday in each week.

JOHN WORKMAN'S REPLY TO MR. C. E. PARKER. Mr. Parker refuses to answer my questions until I ans ?ger his. Of course, it is ever so much easier to pull down than to construct, and he chooses the easier. I cannot offer any excuse for the' fog' he complains of. Mental capacity, as he has p ointed out, differs so much in individuals. I would suggest that he should read my letter yet a third time—seeing that the " fog " had begun to lift after the second reading. On previous occasions be has with some difficulty divined my meaning after sundry attempts and it may be that a little more concentration will again reward his efforts. However, I am going to recapitulate my last reply. I am not desirous of pressing too much upon him but lam anxious that he should follow the tread of the argument. In the first place, I pointed out that he was , wrong in stating that the Christian Socialists opposed , what he terms Modern Socialism with a virile force characteristic of the men. Instead of opposing it they welcomed it. I was not particularly eager to get him , to withdraw that statemont. I oaly hoped that he I would refrain from repeating it. Secondly, I argued that co-operation was necessary an ideal State and for it should be the earnest endeavour of all to work for it. Thirdly, I asked Mr. Parker certain questions so that I might have some reasonable grounds for stating where we agreed and where we parted company so that we might obviate needless dissension and unprofitable correspondence. Mr. Parker seemed to think that, under his system, interest on capital would be possible, and I was anxious to know whether such was the case. However, if I attempt to satisfy him by replying to his questions, in as few words as possible, he will probably tell us exactly what he means by the " whole produce of labour" —whether it stands for Co-operation or Competition. The question is: " How, in the ideal State I have mentioned, individual workers are to be remunerated. Are they to be paid solely according to their needs, or , are efficiency and industry to be taken into account; ' and if they are hew are- the two principles to be harmonized ? ''' The first essential iso.s I have repeatedly mentioned, that each shall give according to his ability. To-day, it is not required of all men that they shall give according to their ability Labour is delegated to some whilst others are content to re nein idle. Idle- ness is common. If each individual was compelled to work according to his ability, effi;iency and industry would be corn non. And if all men gave of their bast, why should they not receive accordiag to their needs? But Mr. Parker is anxious to know whether some, would get more pay than others. To-day, worker are " selected " hap-hazard. Hinds are wanted' Skilled labour is gradually displaced by machinery Quantity of output is of more itngortanee, speaking generally, than quality. It is only necessary to say that you can take any " line " you like—manufacture, art or service. They are all tending to the same goal profit. Profit is becoming of , more importance than -..„,._ good honest work. I have a friend who is a collector of antiques. The other day, I asked why old Ifurniture, old prints, 011 pictures, old china are so much soaght after. He told me that in the "old " days workers put their soul into their work and gave of their best ; to-day," pot-boiling "-was the rule and not the exception. Men to-day, with few exceptions, do not choose their work. It would be better for the community if they did ; and I am of opinion that if some system could be raised whereby the work could be properly allocated it would be beneficial to the State as well as the individual. A thorough system of education will doubtless do much to s dye that problem to some extent. Mr. J. L. Paton, headmaster of the Manchester Grammar School, at the Ardwick Lads' Cub, referred to boy apprentices, whom he said did not leara as much now as they used to do. The vast inaportaece of the years of adolescence was being recognised by social workers. tinder the present system a boy was taken up at the age of 13, when he most needed guidance, and dropped in the street of life with the words," Swim if you can." The natural result was the hooliera. If Mr. Parker and " Perplexed " will seriously think of the possibilities under a system where profit and interest and idleness would be unknown, where " things " would. be made for use and not for profit, they will see th it the " luxuries " " Perplexed " enumerates will no longer be luxuries. " Time was when the shuttle was thrust in and out of all the thousand threads of the warp and it was long to do; but now the spring-staves go up and down as the man's feet move, and this tad that leaf of the warp cometh forward and the shuttle goeth in one shot through all the thousand warps. Yea, so it is that this multiplieth a man many times." Under the present competitive system some should and do get more than others. Industrims men deserve more than idle men ; and yet, they do not always get more. Rich idle men are neither better nor worse than poor idle men who will not work. They are both equally detrimental to the health of a State. The system I advocate will rid the community of all drones. Idleness will be treated as a disease. And if it is thought that some particularly industrious individuals are deserving of special remuneration it is not at all improbable that the then enlightened cona- munity will recognize them in some way that will satisfy the most avaricious -if there are then any such. In conclusion, let me add that whilst iv`e are struggling to get the better of each other let us not forget that there is .a vast difference between property and human life ; and that we are continually being told that this life is only a preparatory stage for the groat hereafter. We do lots of things in this competitive age that are irksome and do not coincide with our Christian principles. Are we to change our Christian principles or our system of Government? I should be glad if Mr. Parker would tell us. In my next reply I shall probably deal with the Economic side of Socialism. JOHN WORKMAN. RAILWAY CAPITAL AND NATIONALIZATION Sir,—ln reply to your correspondent" F.A." if he will kindly read the second paragraph in the letter to which he refers he ;ill see that he misrepresents me (no doubt unwittingly) when he says " Mr. Parker would have us believe that only the land monopoly stands in the way of the railway worker getting the full reward of his labour." It is a pity that your correspondent in quoting from Mr. Money did not give the figures so that we could assess the importance of the point he raises. The figures are as follows : —Railway Capital, £1,282,801,000; less amount included in the fore- going which is nominal only; (i.e. " watered "stock) £104,341,000 ; total, £1,083,400,000. Mr. Money gives the average return as 3 1-3 per cent. against my 3-. Adopting Air. Money's figure if we wipe out the amount shown as " watered " capital it would raise the dividend on actual capital to 4 per cent. The argument of the railway directors would therefore still hold good which was that to give the advance in wages asked for to all grades would not only cause a large depreciation of thee:vital which they held in trust, but would mike it impossible for them to raise any further capital for necessary extensions. It is well also to point out that while some stocks have been inflated, other stocks are almost worthless as far as dividend-earning is concern !d. About seventy-eight millions of railway capital is not receiving a penny in dividends, while altogether rail- way stocks are standing at under the par value, as given above. lam a trustee for shares which have not paid a cent for years and which if realized would involve a serious loss to the estate. F.A. will see from above figures that while the point he has raised is of some importance (especially if the depreciation is left out of account) it shrinks into very small dimensions when compared with the effect of land monopoly or railway costs. See my last letter. Would it not be well for reformers who desire tol secure for labour its full reward to concentrate their attention on the main issue and one that is clear, and net dissipate their energies on minor and question- able points. If we are to accomplish anything in the way of reform there must be concentration on few issues, and in the selection of these issues it is important to choose the one which takes the most from labour of its legitimate reward. The above facts and figures suggest a difficulty

which the country would have to face if the nationalization of Railways were entertained. For this country to have to pay £1,282,801,000 or even the reduced amount of £1,053,460,000 would be bad business. It would be far better to leave the present holders of railway stocks to face the depreciation in values which they risked in taking the shares. I am not blind to the advantages which would arise from national economies which might be affected by the nation by the elimination of a certain. amount of competition, but for the country to nationalize the Railways at anything like the above figures would probably mean an enormous loss, even if they could run them cheaper which I gravely doubt. Some might say that we should only give for the Railway the depreciated value at which the stocks now stand. But here the question of right and wrmg at once comes in. Ido not know that the question of the individual position of those who hold railway stocks ought to be considered, but it is well to remember that neit to Consuls, Railway Stocks are the most c )nvenient form for the invest- ments of the comparatively poor. The rich capitalist has opportunities to invest in more remunerative industrial concerns which if more risky yield a bigger return. The savings of the poor are naturally placed in gilt edged securities, such as Railway Guaranteed Stock. To insist that these should ba surrendered to the State at their present lo v values would mean enormous losses to organizations which collect and invest the savings of the workers such as Trades Unions, Friendly Soc-qeties,Trust Investments,Co-opera- tive Societies and the like, as well as to inlay small individual investers.

Suppose F. A. had saved as the result of his labour £lOO and a few years ag ) bad invested it in ffidland Guaranteed 21 per cent. stock? - Probably he would have paid for this about £lOO The value of the stock now stands at £7O, but F. A. would still say I am still earning 2; per cent. interest; it does' not matter to me what it now stands at for my interest is guaran- teed. If the country forces F. A. to sell his £lOO stock for £7O and gives him Consuls in its place it robs him of £3O and instead of getting £2 103. interest per annum on his new security he will only get £1 15s. To right one wrong by doing another is not a method which will conimend itself to the English people. _ _ . _ _ _ _

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.

"Claudian." What memories of the late Wilson Barrett have been aroused this week at the Royal Court Theatre ! The performance of his great creation, " Claudian" com- pelled one's recollection of Wilson Barrett's visit to Warrington in "The Sign of the Cross." Moreover, the title role was taken by an actor —Mr. William Maelaren—who greatly resembles the famous actor- manager in face, form, and manner,while the play itself is not without points of resemblance to the earlier pro- duction. " Claudian " is a play of the period of Roman greatness in the early centuries of the Christian era. The scene of the prologue is Byzantium, where Claudian figures as a rich, powerful and profligate noble. The curtain rises on a representation of the slave-market, where the merciless Claudian outbids Theorus, a young sculptor, for the possession of a slave who is really the latter's wife. Entreaties are of no avail,and the malignant possessor of the slave-girl pursues her even into the Sanctuary, where he ruthlessly stabs the priest who would stand between them. The priest with his dying breath, condemns Claudian to live in perennial youth, unloved and cursed by a fate that shall turn every attempted good deed to death or disaster. One hundred years is stippeeed to elapse, and we see Claudian as Governor of Charydos. Outwardiy he is still the same, but in character he has become gentle, just, and melancholy. The curse pursues him, he is unable to atone by good deeds. Befriending a poor girl on the roadside results in the death of her child, and his attempt to help Almida by procurine the release of her lover causes the girl to go suddenly blind. 'Before this affliction, however, Almida falls in love with Claudinn, and in the end his love for her brings about his redemption. In a scene of great power he stands among the ruins of his palace and chooses between love and the perpetuity of the curse and death and divine redemption, his final choice being the act of a great abnegation. Almida's sight returns to her, and with it her honest love for Agazil, the blacksmith. Mr. Ifardaren acts with great skill in the difficult part of Mau iian, rising alternately to heights of passion and, falling to depths of despair. - He has earned the wannest praise from large audiences this week, and a better °la-Lilian could not be desired. An accomplished performance is also given by Miss, Lily C. Bindmann, as Arnilia, though one is not con- vinced that she is best suited by the part. The villain of the piece is Thariogalus, tetrarch of Charydos, a blue-beard-like individual whom Claudian thwarts and finally condemns to death. Mr. F. Owen , Chambers was seen to advantage in this part and pur- sued his wicked career with telling energy. Mr. Douglas Earle was capital as the simple but manly blacksmith, and a word of praise is also due to Mr. Weston Hubbard for his easy and natural acting as Alcoves, a wealthy farmer, and the father of Ahnida. The comic element of the play was provided by the love passages besweenße.os and Edesea, and in these two roles Mr. C. T. Chaloner and Miss gaud Garth were admirable. Mr. Chaloner is a true:humorist and his mimicry provoked roars of laughter. The play is splendidly mounted, and the earthquake and elemental convulsion which destroy Claudian's palace are a triumph of stage craft The lightning flashes, the thunder peals, and then with a reverberating roar, which makes half the audience exclaim, the structure of the palace falls into ruins. It is one of the finest spectacles ever seen on a Warrington stage. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. Next week should be a busy one at the above theatre. Messrs. Askew and Knoblaugh's drama " The Shulamite " will oecupy the stage. This play was first produced at the Savoy Theatre, London. It is a South African story, and all the scenes are laid about the farmhouse and outbuildings of a Boer farmer, Simeon Krillett, a stern and implacable old , Puritan. He has married a y mug Cape girl for his second wife and leads her a miserable life. Unfortu- nately the Boer has an -Eeglishm in in his employ as overseer, one Robert Waring. The rest of the pla I may be easily imagined. Simeon Keillkt,t, the over- bearing farmer is played by gr. Algernon J. Hicks; E and Deborah, the Boer's second wife, by Miss Ella Thornton.

OVER FIFTY TREES DESTROYED. -- Indignation Meeting. The largo room at the Hall Cafe, St ,cktort Heath, was the scene of an triusual meeting on Thursday evening. It was called at the instance of the Tree. Planting Com nitte,e to consider what action should be taken in face of the deprelati)ns of some person or persons who during Wednesday night practically destroyed between fifty and sixty of the trees plaated by the committee in Fairfield-road, Whitefield-road, and Cawdor-st:.eet. The meeting included nearly the whole of the members of the Tree Planting Cammittee and the Parish Council. The greatest indignation was manifested at the vandalism which had been so ruthlessly committed and it was the general opinion that no pains should be spared to bring the offender or offenders to justice. Speeches were made by the Chairman (Ur. C. Plinston), Messrs. Bouchier, Clarke, Brown, Biudloss and Hickman and many strong ,things were said. Ultimately a resolution was passed that a reward of £2O be offered for information leading to the dis- covery of the person or persons responsible for the damage, and the bulk of the z£2o was guaranteed at the meeting.

Animated Pictures at Parr Hall. There have beea large audiences at. the Parr Hall this week, the occasion being the visit of Mr. R. Pringle's North American Picture Company. The Thaw case is thrown on the screen, and great interest was taken in the pictures., several incidents in this sensational drama of real life being depicted. Another very attractive item is" A. race for millions," which tells the story of a woman's revenge. The most humorous is "The heavenly twins," whilst another good picture is " John D. the Reporter" The event of the evening is provided by the unique singing and talking pictures, whilst Mr. Charles Clifford enter- tains the audience on the harp. He also playa a small Irish harp which was made in the year 1784. . Much praise is clue to the band which accompanies the numerous productions. There will be peiformanees this afternoon and again to-night at 8.

div.head: WARRINGTON WORKS ROBBERY.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKS ROBBERY.
Prisoners Committed for Trial.

The adjourned case of stealing and receiving large quantities of bras was heard at the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, when William Powers, furi3aceman, School-brow, and Henry Perkins, labourer, of Bank- street, were charged with braakin., and entering the fitting shop of the Whitecross Works and stealing 1181 b. of brass, value £5. Joseph Matthews, broker, of Lythgoes-lane, who was arrested in court at the first hearing on Friday, was charged with receiving the brass, knowing it to have been stolen. Mr. T. S. Steel, who prosecuted, stated that at noon on Saturday, November 23, the foreman of the fitting shop securely fastened the door leading to that depart- ment. Next morning the door was found open and a quantity of brass missing. The matter was reported to the police, who from inquiries found that the two prisoners Powers and Perkins visited the house of Matthews and offered for sale a quantity of brass. Matthews was not at home on the first visit, but later in the evening he saw the two men and gave them 38s. for the brass without asking a single question as to how the prisoners came by it. When arrested Powers and Perkins admitted the robbery, but denied breaking and entering the shop, as they stated the door. was not locked.
Corroborative evidence was given in support of this statement.

It was alleged by Perkins that Matthews knew the brass was stolen, but of the purchase-money (365.) he (Perkins) gave him 6s. back. Matthews handed in a statement which was read by Mr. Jenkins who appeared on his behalf. HO stated that he had carried on the business of a metal broker for five or six- years, and for the past two years at Pump-yard, Lythgoes-lane. When he got home he found Perkins and Powers waiting in the kitchen. He was told that the men had brought some brass. He asked what kind of br ass it was, and said she thought it was machinery brass. She told him a young wonfrin named Wild, in this employ, it was 811 b. weight. It bad been. the custom for his

div.head: BLANK_ CHEQUE
div.p: BLANK_ CHEQUE

with which to go into the House to delude and mislead the people. He was glad the country refused, and he hoped they would always refuse to give either a Liberal or a Tory Government a blank cheque, because it was a most dangerous thing. No Government ever went into power more pledged and no Government had more honestly tried to fulfil that pledge than the present Government. (Hear, hear.) It had done more for the vvorkingclasses than any Government that ever sat in St. Stephen's. (Applause.) It had been the old watchword of the Liberal party to legislate for the greatest good of the greatest number and they had carried that out in its entirety. They were.always told by the Tories that the trade of the County was bad under a Liberal Government—in fact Lord Lansdowne said there was "no alternative Government," ridiculing the idea that the country was going to return anybody but the Tories. But the country had found an alternative Government which had won the admira- tion of the whole world.. England to-day was as solidly for Free Trade as it was at the General Election. (Applause.) There was to be no tampering with tariffs. The best trade the country ever knew was under Mr. Gladstone's Government in 1871-2-3—(applause)—and England was witnessing prosperity now which he hoped would long continue. In 1903-4 one penny in the £ income tax yielded £2,562,551 ; in 1904-5, £2,580,533; 1905-6, £2,12,500; 1906-7.. £2,633,338 —the last figure being the highest yield for any year known in British his,tory. And that was under a Liberal Government. (Applause.) When the Tories imposed the-

div.head: COAL TAX
div.p: COAL TAX

he prophesied that it would mean a reduction in wages and short time. In less than six months there was alO per cent. redaction and the men were losing a day per weak. We had enough coal in this country to last 500 years at our present production of 250,000,000 tons per annum. The Liberal Government had abolished the tax with the result that the men had got back their ten per cent. and the trade was prosperous. The romoval of the tax had nothing to •do with the high price of coal, for he knew that the price to-day at the pit mouth did not amount to Bs. 6d. a ton. They would have to tackle another question at the base of this. The Tories would try to lead them off on a false scent, but there was no one in the House on the progressive side who did not agree on the matter. There were only two lobbies and they would go into one against the Tories on it. Somebody in this country was having something for nothing, and they meant to stop it. (Applause.) The Tories would try to perpetuate it and continue to see that men who had plenty should have more. They believed that" to him that bath shall be given." The progressive forces would have to tackle the -

div.head: ROYALTY RIGHTS
div.p: ROYALTY RIGHTS

of this country if they were going to have progress. (Applause.) On the continent of Europe, taking Germany, France, Belgium, Austria. and Bavaria, they paid lid. per ton royalty on coal; 7d. on pig iron ; and 13d. on steel. In England we had to pay. 6d. a ton on coal, 4s. 6d. on pig iron, and 6s. 6d. on steel. But there was also the difference that on the Continent the royalties went to the Chancellor of the Exchequer to meet taxation.whereas ours went to into pockets of the landlords, and that was where they were getting some- thing for nothing. (Applause.) If the present Chancellor of the Exchequer wanted to know where he was going to get the money from to provide old age pensions—because there must be no hesitation about this—(applause)—there were those in the House who wonld have the courage to tell him that there was a source of revenue he must tap. (Applause.) It would not injure anybody, but it would bring back

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
St. Peter's Church Army Mission.

The anniversary service in connection with the above Mission was held on Sunday evening. The preacher was the Rev. H. Russell. His address was listened to with great interest by a large congregation. The hymns were sung most heartily and Captain Higson conducted the service, Mr. Callan reading the lesson. On Monday evening in the sclool, the annual tea meeting took place when tea was served in an admirable manner by the lady friends of the mission, to the evident satis- faction of all present. The meeting was presided over by Councillor Steel, churchwarden, who spoke most highly of the Work of the mission in the parish, and expressed the deep regret of them all at the departure shortly of Captain Higson from amongst them, his term of office as officer Evangelist in St. Peter's Parish for three years being almost expired. He wished him God speed in his newly appointed parish. He earnestly appealed to all present to support the work of the mission in their midst. The Vicar (Rev. B. Percival), expressed his deep gratituee to the Church Army for training Godly laymen and women to work in parishes under the direction of the incumbents, and said how much they owed in their parish to the officers in the past who have worked so loyally, and been of such great, help in that crowded parish. He joined with the Chair- man in the expression of the regret of himself and the parishioners that Captain Higson was shortly to leave. Mr. Gibson spoke of his long experience in connection with the Church Army, and its successful efforts in winning the working men and women where the ordinary parochial efforts failed. He appealed to all to take an active part in mission work in their parisb. The Rev. H. Russell congratulated the workers upon the noble work they were doing, and assured them of his earnesit prayers, and practical support. The Warrington Thursday Glee Party rendered the Glees : "Perfect in Christ " "The Little Church " " Lead Kindly Light under the leadership of Mr. E. Roberts. Solos were given by Mr.Foriter and oboe selections by Mr. Stanley. Mr. F. Webster was the accompanist. All the items were enthusiastically received by the audience. Votes of thanks to the Chairman, speakers, artistes and donors to the tea, and the ladies who had so successfully carried out the arrangements, was proposed by Mr. Wratislaw, who thanked the clergy and parishioners for their hearty welcome to him in his Christian work amongst them. Mr. Webb in seconding,mentioned that the spirit of unity had happily prevailed amongst them in the mission. Captain Higson thanked all for this great kindness whilst amongst them. He thanked God for the great opportunities earnest laymen had in the Church Army for evangelistic work. Messrs. Greaves, and Taylor, also were present.

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.

The thirty-second anniversary in connection with this Church were held on Sunday when the Rev. Marmaduke Riggall. who at one time belonged to this circuit, occupied the pulpit. In the morning the preacher took for his subject." Love," and he said that when they bad the love of Christ in their hearts they had a great incentive for work in any sphere. The anthem "The King of Love my Shepherd is" was rendered by the choir. In the afternoon Mr. Riggall addressed the Senior Men's Bible Class at Silver-street Wesleyan schools and related some of his experiences in New Zealand four years ago, when he had the pleasure of meeting several persons with whom he had been acquainted while in the Warrington Circuit. In the evening at Bewsey-road Church Mr. Riggall gave an exposition from the first Psalm. On Monday evening Mr. Riggall gave an address on " Character " in the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church. Mr. John Bennett, formerly of Padgate, presided and the Rev. Sidney Pitt was also present. The Rev. M. RIGGALL gave several illustrations of character. He likened it to the image and superscrip- tion on a coin. Reputation was one phase of character, but character was permanent. Writing was character. The word character did not appear once in the English Bible. If a man had a good character he would be able to stand the tests which were put before him. Character was asserting itself. It was stronger than the might of the sword and the eloquence of skilful oratory. Character was invisible, yet it was of active power. Good character bad God on its side, and nobody wanted more than that. The lecture was both interesting and instructive, and a vote of thanks was accorded to the Lecturer, on the motion of Mr. GUEST, seconded by Mr. UPSON.—A vote of thanks was also accorded te Mr. Bennett for presiding and to the choir for their assistance. The collections, which were taken by the trustees themselves,were in aid of the Trust Funds.

THE CONGO ATROCITIES. At this stage the following question was handed in : Will Mr. Harvey give his opinion about the Congo atrocities and as to whether Leopold has kept his part in the treaty of Berlin? Mr. HARVEY replied : The atrocities are an abomina, tion and Leopold has not kept his promises. (Applause.) -VOTES OF THANKS. Mr. WYNNE JONES moved a vote of thanks to the speakers and said he was sure the members .of the League would do all they could to strengthen the hands of Mr. Crosfield in backing up the Government. The House of Lords question had to be settled before any lasting good could be done, but be hoped the Govern- ment would not appeal to the country until they had got all they could for tho welfare of the ,country. There were measures they could pass in spite of the Lords. (Applause.) MT. ATKINSON seconded. Mr. C. E. PARKER supported. He said they had got a grand Government and its record was a splendid one. They must not let the enthusiasm which! was generated p tyl S onris at the last election wane but maintain it so that the • promises and expectations which were held out to them e at the election would have a fair chance of realization. ; (Applause.) The vote was heartily passed and a similar compliment to the chairman concluded the meeting.

div.p: MY DEAR
How are the Christmas contributions pro- gressing? I hope you are all doing your utmost to _send me a great many. .

,s Our League is now lager than ever befrre, so naturally I expect to receive many more than last year. So many letters have come to hand during this week, that I have not had time to deal with every one, and, besides, our columns would not hold all.

During last week I visited a most delightful little place called Beccles, in Suffolk—quite near Yarmouth; I wonder if any of you know this place l All the country is looking very wet and forlorn, although there are still a good many leaves on the trees. Winter is coming, z..nd that most welcome time will soon arrive of holidays and Christmas fun. Well, before the end of this month I hope to have a lot of nice warm things for my poor children. I will acknowledge contributions in my next week's letter. With lots of love,
UNCLE NED.
Dear Uncle Ned,—l should very much like to join your C.C.L. We have got a dog named Rover, and I arn sending you a piece of poetry, entitled " Rover's Fault." ROVER'S FAULT.

Our Rater is a dear bow-bow, He's worth his weight in gold; He guards the house, he drives the cow, And does just what he's told. I:€t Rover has one fault, you see; When we go out to play, He runs and jumps and barks with glee, But not a word he'll say. Loften tell him, in his ear, A story, just for fun, And he will sit quite still to hear, And wait till I have done. But if I ask him then tell A story of his own, He N7,-Gnt; and yet I feed him well And give him many a bone. NEVILLE SCOTT.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l have such a beautiful pet cat. Every morning it is at the door wait- ing for us to let her in. It follows us all about the yard, and it comes after me to school. It is a tortoiseshell cat; it has three white legs, and one black and white. It will catch rats and mice and play with them in the yard. It sleeps in a box that I made for it. We had a eat before this one, and it had some kittens, and it is one of its kittens. It is one year and a-half old, and its weight seven pounds and a- half, and its name is Mull-Tib. It comes up- stairs to us, and lays on the bed until we get up. When lam having my breakf.ast it will come and sit on my shoulder. If I stroke it on the back it will jump up and creep all up to my head. We are all fond of it, as my parents like us to be kind to God's creatures. CECIL SAUNBY.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l have such a lovely little pig. It is supposed to be white, but it gets dirty. I brought it up with a baby's bottle, and it follows me about like a child when it wants its meals. Its mother died when it was a baby. It comes in our kitchen, but mother drives it out. People call pigs silly, but I am sure they are not. This one understands every word, and will come directly I call. CECIL FISHER.
Dear Uncle Ned,—For my pet I have a dear little kitten. It is a grey with one patch of white on it. At night I get a long prece of

string with a cork on the end. and hold of it, and has such fun. In the morning scmetimes I find the kitten trying to get into mv boots. Then it follows me to school, and I have to take,it back again. At dinner-time I have to feed it, also at tea-time. If I was not looking where the kitten was before I went out, she would be sure to follow me. I have tied a piece of pink ribbon round its neck. It was given to me by auntie. It is only five weeks, old. I do love it so much; I couldn't part with it. It is so old-fashioned. I think this is all I have to tell you about my dear •little kitten, so good-bye. LILY LUNN.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l have got such lovely pet pigeons. They ,are pure white, and are tumblers. When they go in the air they shine like silver. They come into the room and perch on the chairs, waiting to be fed, and will let me stroke them. But next door there is a vicious bird who pecks the young ones to death. I am afraid when they are in the room the cat. will catch them, as they do not seem to mind her being there in the least._
GERTRUDE FISHER

1 Dear Uncle Ned,—l have such a nice pet kitten. Its name is Daisy. It follows me to chapel, and they have to turn it out. I tie a nice ribbon round its neck. and it looks so pretty. It is tortoiseshell. It comes running upstairs every morning and lies down in bed. I dress it up like a doll, and it sits up in the chair to tea. I put a bib round its neck and teach it to behave well. I brush its long fur out and keep. it , clean.
ETHEL STURTON.

It's so hard to be sick with the mumps, mamma! Tell me a story. A make-believe one that just couldn't happen! That will make me forget." And mamma took Donald on her lap and told him this story: . "Once there was a little boy who was lame, and very, very tired of keeping still. "It was a summer day, warm and beautiful. Overhead the clouds were so white and fleecy in the blue sky, and they floated so dreamily, that the little boy's eyes followed them wist- fully. "'1 wish I could sail a. little way on one!'" . _ _ _
"As he looked he thought, 'I will sail on one,' and he seized his little crutch and very slowly climbed a high hill at the back of his house.

"The clouds floated on the very top, he knew, and when he reached it, a dear little cloud, was there waiting for him. "Up, over, in, he was nestled in the soft white cloud and ready to sail. "The air was cooler than on the earth, but he pulled a bit of cloud round him, and it was soft as a lamb's back. "And he sailed—far, far away!
"Past green fields and over thick foreste, over bright rivers and lakes, and his cheeks grew pink and his eyes shone like stars at all he saw.

"And then it began to grow dark. "Lovely colours were tin the sky, which changed to deep, dull blues—and then a tiny moon crept out and a few beautiful stars, and then this little cloud p.assepger grew sleepy and hungry, too, and said, 'Now, it is time for me to go back to my own mother.' _

"And it --was wonderftil all the time, for the cloud dropped lower, lower, until it was again at the top of the hill behind this little boy's house and he softly slid out and over, and went Clown the hill to his own mother. There, that is a story that couldn't have happened! Did it make you forget,- Donald?" asked mother. But Donald was asleep. Another little passenger was starting toward the land of happy dreams. -
A NAUGHTY DOLLY.
"Tick—tock! tick—tock!" said the solemn old clock in the corner.

"You're an awful drawly old clock!" said Dolly, spitefully, out of her corner. Auntie had put her there because she went to the plum-sauce again, and she was to stay there just "fifteen minutes by the clock and think of her Sins."
I'm afraid she thought a great deal more of the plum-sauce a.nd "the drawly clock" than she did of her sins.

"Tick—tock 1 I'm going to mock you, old clock!" said Dolly, sticking her tongue out and making horrible facie. "You're just mean to go ticking on slowest you ever did in your life to keep me here. I'll mock every word you say!" And Dolly began mocking the solemn "tick— tock," bobbing her head back and forth and from side to side, as if she thought it would hurt the clock's feelings. But the clock didn't care. He had ticked off too many half-hours for little children on that very lower stair to feel sensitive about their little remarks.

All at once the little bobbing head grew still, and the little mocking tongue stuck in the middle of a " tick-tock," and Dolly was fast asleep. And when she woke up the old clock held up his fore-finger and pointed to the time. and his round old face actually seemed to laugh at her, to think she had punished hereelf by stay- ing in that corner three-quarters of an hour instead of one.
"It's just the way!" said Dolly. "I always get punished worscr when I don't take it pleasant the first time. I won't be bad to you any more, old clock." Lo she did think of her sine, after all.
C. Do.
FROM JOHN 0' GROAT'S TO LAND'S END. Every one has heard the expression, "From John o' Groat's to Land's End," and knows that it means "from one end of Britain to the other."

John o' Groat's House would not have been so famous if its owner had not built it in a very peculiar manner. It is said that he had eight sons, and to prevent them quarrelling, he built his house with eight. sides, eight Windows, and eight doors, and placed within an eight-sided table. _ _ _

It was situated on the west side of Duncansby Head, a cape on the extreme north-west of Scotland. The site is clearly marked on the turf, and an hotel has been built close to the place. Land's End is a rocky promontory on the extreme south-east of England; in short, it is the end of Britain, for it is farther out than any cape on the south of England. If a man were to walk from John o' Groat's to Land's End in as direct a line as possible, he would pass through no fewer than nineteen counties. The first part of his walk would be across fiat moors, for although the coast of Caithness is bold and rocky, there is an exten- sive moorland in the ,north of the county; and the last part would be through the county of Cornwall, which is largely occupied by granite mountains, And hills of slaty rock.

Paris has not only witnessed the discovery of a new chemical clement, as has often been the case before, but has now the distinction of giving her name to the discovery. Ytterbium is one of the rare, earths which have already yielded actinium, polonium, and radium.

div.head: LIGHTNING OF VESUVIUS.
div.p: THE LIGHTNING OF VESUVIUS.

Among the remarkable phenomena- con- nected with the great eruption of Vesuvius, in April, .1906, - Professor Matteucci, in a re- port to the -Italian Geological Society, men- tions the electric 'discharges in the huge column of smoke, gas, and steam that rose, swaying with the wind, thousands of feet above the crater. Many discharges took place between the column of smoke and the earth, and these are described as having been of extraordinary intensity. The greatest measured height of the column during the eruption was about 42,600 ft., or, in round numbers, eight miles.

div.head: LIFE IN SEVERED HEADS.
div.p: LIFE IN SEVERED HEADS.

Every angler knows the extraordinary tenacity to, life that is occasionally shewn by the severed head of a fish. An eel's head will afford an excellent illustration. Professor A. Bulabko, of Tomsk, well known for his re- searches on the resuscitation of the heart long after its apparent death, shewed a gathering of medical men recently a simple method of pouring what is known as Locke's fluid through the surviving head" of a fish, separated from the body and freely exposed to air. The brain of the fish seems to require a fair exchange of gases. The activity of the brain centres can be maintained for many hours, and, indeed, by this method can be re- stored after complete extinction.

div.head: WHEN THE EARTH DRIES UP.
div.p: WHEN THE EARTH DRIES UP.

In addition to being burnt up by fire or frozen to an icicle, there is another cause of destruction threatening us. That the earth is gradually drying up is the conclusion reached by the French geologist M. Martel. He has made careful observations of subterranean caverns. They contain, he says, not only the secret of prehistoric life, inasmuch as they were the homes of men of the remotest age, but also bear indications of the endless future. M. Martel has found proof of a steady k fall i the level of the water in these sub- terra an depths, and from this fact he con- clude that the world will eventually become depopu ated through the failure of the water supply, and, finally, become a dried-up planet.

div.head: CANAL FORMED OF STEEL PLATES.
div.p: CANAL FORMED OF STEEL PLATES.

A description is given in the Revue Mine- rallurgique of a canal for irrigation purposes, to serve a district between Assuan and Ed- pore in _Egypt, bordered on one side by the Nile and on the other by the Desert. This is an absolutely waterless country, where no rain has fallen for a period of from 3,000 to 4,000 years, and in order to prevent percola- tion into the arid soil the main canal bring- ing the water, which is 1,750 yards in length, is formed of steel plates in. thick, riveted together. It is nearly semi-circular in sec- tion, the diameter of the circle being 23ft. As it has only to convey the water, and the water surface will not be used, it is tied across the top and also round the outside by T iron flanges, placed transversely to the axis, and spaced about 2ft. 6in. apart, with stiffening pieces fixed across the channel obliquely to the direction of the flow. It is stated that the -ironwork was put together in situ, and entailed the. use of 650,000 rivets. Provision has been made for expansion and contraction, and the total- length is divided into seventeen sections with sliding joints in masonry chambers.

div.head: IS FROZEN MEAT SAFE?
div.p: IS FROZEN MEAT SAFE?

Dr. Thomas, medical officer of health for Stepney, makes some important observations regarding• frbzen meat. Cold, he says, does not always kill the putrefactive germs. They possess an unusual resi6tina° power against low temperatures, but thi resistance does not in any way militate against the preservative effect of the cold. Though tl,.e germs are not destroyed by cold, the low temperature prevents their multiplication, and in this dormant condition the develop- ment of their action is prevented. When frozen meat is thawed and exposed on a hot day in the window or on a board in front of a shop it soon becomes tainted, because the dormant

GERMS AGAIN BECOME ACTIVE, a—.d multiply. When tainted, the meat may either be canned or minced and converted into sausages. If intended for sausages a colouring matter is frequently added to give it a fresh appearance. Oxide of iron, or some of the aniline dyes, are used for this purpose. Spices and sweet herbs are also added that the tainted smell and taste are disguised, and it is impossible to state whether the meat is unfit to eat or not. Its consumption may be followed, Dr. Thomas rightly points out, by disastrous results.

div.head: TIN IN THE STARS.
div.p: TIN IN THE STARS.

Since Sir William and Lady Huggins, in the observatory at the back of their Tulse Hill residence, founded half a century ago the science of astrophysics by spectroscopic observation of the stars, the spectroscope has shewn us that many of the elements found on the earth are also present in the stars billions of miles away. Thus astrono- mers are able to identify in many of the stars such common terrestrial elements as sodium, magnesium, hydrogen, iron, and cal- cium. But only quite recently has the pre- sence of tin been suspected. Mr. Goatcher, one of the staff of the Royal Observatory at the Cape, examining spectrograms of the bright red star Antares in Scorpio (" The Heart of the Scorpion "), found a discord- ance in the wave-length of a particular line in the spectrum, and after careful measure- ments he and his tolleagues became con- vinced that the discrepancy could only be due to the presence of a tin line, the wave- length of which is, according to the most re- liable authorities,. the same as that of the mysterious line in the spectrum of Antares. Should further investigation confirm the conclusions of the Cape astronomers this will be the first time that tin has ever been identified in the atmosphere of a star.
LIGHT AS A HEALTH MAKER.
Light starvation is one of the most serious

affliclions of the human race, says Mr. W. J. IM`Gee, former President of the American t Anthropological Association, writing in the New York Tribune. It is indeed the fruitful cause ot a multitude of physical ills. Strange does it &ern that the function of light as a maker of health should have been ignored to so great an extent. Its hygienic usefulness seems to be almost unrecognised to-day by the medical faculty. A physician sends his patients to the sea shore, and at the end of . a few weeks they come back to town with a .
gratifying augtrientation of health and vigour. The improvement is attributed to . . _ _ _ .
the incidental chaiige of diet and scene. In a measure this idea is correct; but the truth is that exposure to light hae been the chief means of cure. Light is Nature's

MOST IMPORTANT CURATIVE AGENCY. It is often said that there is nothing like plenty of fresh air and exercise to make people Well and keep them so;— but, while this is true enough. the benefit obtained is due mainly to the incidental exposure to unlimited light. A game of lawn tennis is a light bath; a row on the river is a light bath; a bath in the sea is at the same time a bath of light, which is one reason why it is so healthful. Young people at the seaside try their best, as they say, to "get a coat of tan," for which purpose they expose themselves as much as possible to the sun- shine ; and when the tan has been acquired they exhibit it proudly as a sign of health. They do this without knowinn the reason why, because tan, which is the result of free exposure to a glare of lfght, is associated in everybody's mind with physiol vigour aad "tooling sood.,'L
ODDFELLOWSHIP IN THE WARRINGTON DISTRICT.
Visit G# the Grand Master.

The "Prince of Wales" lodge of the Independent Order of Oddfellows (Manchester Unity) was honoured on Saturday evening with the visit of Bro. Dempsey of i Eccles who s Grandmaster of the Order. The meeting was thrown open and there was a very large attendance at the Pelican Hotel. The chair was occupied by Bro. T. P. Bradshaw, P.P.G.M., who was supported by Bro. Dempsey to whom a warm welcome was offered. Bro. W. MASON in replying to the toast "Prosperity , to the Eccles District ' said the Eccles district owed a great debt of gratitude to Warrington and other districts for the help and encouregement they had given them, and he thanked the Warrington District for the way he bad been received. The toast of the "Warrington District" was pro- posed by Bro. Walsh, P.G.M., who also referred to the kind way they had been received. Bro. MIo.SEY, P.P.G.M., in responding to the toast in the absence of Bro. Brooks, D.G.M. of the Warring- ton District,said they had; not been so successfnl during the past year numerically but they were in a good financial position. Several of the lodges were quite solvent and the last quinquinial valuation showed that others were on the point of becoming in a similar position, and he firmly believed that at the next valua- tion there would be a little surplus. (Applause.) Bro .WEBSTER, C.S., proposed the "Board of Directors of the Manchester Unity," in which he referred to the satisfaction which Bro. Dempsey had given them. At this stage Bro. BRADSHAW presented Bro. Dempsey with a gold-mounted umbrella, on behalf of the Warrington District, as a slight token of their esteem and appreciation for him. Bro. DEMPSEY, in returning thanks, said that he had received a large number of presents lately. It was something to be proud of that they were members of Burl a society as the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows. (Hear, hear.) It had 407 districts, 5,000 lodges, 1,020,000 members, arid supported by a capital of £4,000,000. (Applause.) He was afraid they did not think enough of their position. They seemed to rcst too much on the laurels of the past, but there was much more energy required to-day if they were to maintain and keep unblemished one of the brightest heritages that was ever banded down to working men. They received over £2,000000 in sick and funeral contribu- tions, and distributed over £1,610,000 in sick and funeral claims. In the Warrington district, which had 1,944 members' £1,950 was distributed in 1906. That was sufficient to show the value of the friendly society movement. Ho had been informed that there was a juuenile branch in Warrington with a membership of 2,221, and a capital of £7,502. The juvenile branch was part and parcel of the Lodge, and that a portion of that money could be used to support their poorer lodges. They knew many of the members of the juvenile branch were seniors, and if they regis- tered that branch it would enable the !odges to come out in a sound position at the next valuation. The benevolent funds were a useful and important part of the work of the Unity. The contributions were very small, but the benefits were very large indeed. They should look to their investments, and see that they were placed on a sound footing and that they were getting the highest rate possible with the greatest possible security. The unity was just what the members liked to make it. They had plenty of talent in War- rington to make every lodge bright and cheerful, and if the members knew what to expect then their numbers would increase. He was delighted to know that in Warrington the Education Authorities had recognized the friendly society movement and allowed them a representative on the committee. In this respect they had beaten Eccles. (Applause.) During the evening musical items were given by Bros. J. Willett, Walker, J. Wood end Webster.
