div.head: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
div.p: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.

Infantile Mortality. Sir,—One cannot fail to read the eloquent sermon of the Rev. S. Pitt, aa published in your paper last Satur- day, and not ask oneself the question : How is it such a subject is not more prominently brought before the public by the diffarent clergy of the many parishes in our midst? How is it that the clergy stand by and see our town racked by such a curse? Are not they the first who should cry out against it, as day by day in their midst they see the children of their own particular parish dying through want, arid through neglect, yet never do they appeal to their congregation to tread down the means whereby these little ones are neglected in such a manner as to cause death. So long as our clergy help to return to public posi- tions men whose interest is absolutely with the sale of drink, and allow these men to occupy positions as church officers in their church, so long, I say, we cannot expect this grave question to be fought. The Church of England ministers are ever fond of telling us Sunday after Sunday that they teach the one true faith, and that faith is to cherish and love little children, care for the poor and outcast, yet they never attempt to remove the evil of drink, slum dwellings and other social curses which tend to make the poor and the outcast. Would that more stirring sermons like the Rev. Mr. Pitt's were preached. People would then be brought more face to face with this most burning question, and one might in the near future see Nonconformists and Church of England clergy and laity uniting in one body to bring about such a change as would enable the mothers of the poorer classes to rear their children and to see them growing to man's estate midst surroundings pnre, holy, and healthy. S.J.F.

div.head: Catholics and the Congo.
div.p: Catholics and the Congo.

Sir,—l was assured upon the platform that I might rely upon the fairness of both Fathers Whittle and Wilson. I must confess to feeling that they are not treating the Congo question with quite the broad-mindedness I would like to see. Their criticisms fall mainly into three divisions. (1) Lack of specific detail as to atrocities. (2) The favourable evidence produced by certain " guests " of the Congo State authorities and the British Consul. (3) The good done by the Congo Free State. I With reference to the first point await the accept- ance of my proposal to Father Wilson to make declara- tions before any magistrate with specific detail even more fully than at Parr Hall. At the same time let me again say that it is the system we are fighting against more than specific atrocities which are inevitable. As to the second point. I must confess that I doubt the fairness of my rev, friends to which they lay claim, otherwise when stating that in certain given districts a single consul gives no specific details of atrocities why in the interest of their boasted " fair- ness" did they not quote the following passage from those same consular reports? "The people are all dis- heartened and are unanimously of the opinion that they wer3 better off under the Arabs." To end which domination was the raison d'etre of the Congo Free State. This Arab dominion,Father Whittle tells us,involved the death of 100,000 human beings every year. The last consular report which proves so satis- factory to the rev, gentleman places on record the opinion that the Congo natives were better off under that system of tyranny and bloodshed than the present "humanitarian Government" ! We Congo Reformers are quite satisfied with the last consular reports. As to the last division of Father Whittle's points. We find him actually quoting missionary statistics (which are creditable to the Missionary Societies) as showing what the State has done ! ! I agree that in certain areas the Powers signatory to the Berlin Act have refused to permit the importation to any great extent of intoxicating liquors. It is pro',,ably the one regulation the Congo Free State has o bserved.—l am, yours truly, JOHN H. HARRIS.

Greet Britain Still Forging Ahead. Sir,—The figures given below showing the exports and imports for nine months ending September 30th, 1907, of the principal trading countries, are-of interest. They show that Great Britain's lead is well maintained. Germany alone in percentage increase of exports shows a greater growth, but in value Great Britain's increase is considerably larger. _

EXPORTS. 1906 1907 Increase Inc. £. £. £. p'r Germany 217,618,000 249,261,000 31,643,000 19/o France 153,101,000 164,583,000 11,482,000 7y, United States 253,462,000 272,836,000 19,374,C00 77, United K'gd0m278,054,000 319,281,000 41,227,000 15Z If the calculation were made per head of the popula- tion the rapid development in export trade of this country would be still more striking. It may be of interest in this connection to give the figures per head of the population of the whole foreign trade of the United Kingdom and our three chief competitors since the century began. These years include the period in which we have had to endure the Tariff Reform crusade. 1901-2 1906

-- - per head. per head. Increase. Germany France United States £6 10 0 £8 0 0 .£1 10 0 United Kingdom £IS 0 0 £2l. 0 0 £3 0 0 It will be remembered that one of the most prominent points in Mr. Chamberlain's arguments was that while he did not deny that this country was increasing its trade, this trade, he contended, was not increasing at the same rate as that of Protectionist countries. This was one of ths first notes struck. It was taken up and kept vibrating from a thousand platforms until expand- ing exports smothered the chord. What becomes of it under the light of the above figures? It is well also to consider the character of international trade as well as its volume, and we hold that our foreign trade is more profitable than the corresponding trade of other countries. These block the flow of imports by taxes, and in their exports give bargains at the expense of their own people. They hold up the prices in their own country by aid of tariffs and give the surplus away without profit to outsiders. The out- siders are therefore the ones which derive the chief benefit and this country being the largest buyer gets the most advantage. In England we pick up the bargains of the world. Our export trade rests on a natural basis, plys on its merits, when it ceases to pay we stop exporting. Thus we see that our external trade as a section of the great international barter is healthy and profitable, while much of the goods we get in exchange from Protectionist countries NV9 get at prices which leave no profit to the exporting country, but which to us are extra good value. T have no fear that on this issue alone this country will ever snrrender its advantageous position. What we have to fear and guard against, is a combination of reactionary forces allied with what is naturally and instinctively conservative, landing a party in power the more militant section of which is sinking it deener and deeper in the quagmire of what they call a Fiscal Reform" but think of as Protection. CHARLES E. PARNER. Penketh, December 3rd, 1937.

div.head: Parliamentary Debating Society.
div.p: A Parliamentary Debating Society.

Sir,—With reference to your remarks in tho '" Examiner" dated August 31st, about the old Parlia- mentary Debating Society which existed in Warrington prior to ISSI it would be interesting to know on what lines it was worked. The suggestion as to forming another society has been followed I notice, in a letter to one of your contemporaries, but in a manner which I think will hardly give general satisfaction. Your contem- porary says "The movement has our entire approba- tion." Let us be thankful for this, so far as it goes, bat how far does it go? What party or how much collective opinion does that paper represent? I don't think under the circumstances we can attach much importance to that word "our:". A more practical question is, are tke leaders of all political parties in sympathy with that movement? If they are not, it cannot be a permanent success, and the debates will not be a faith- ful reflex of public opinion. The poor show which Warrington made at the National Service League Debate is a strong argument in favour of such a society, if any were needed, although I don't think the arrangements on that occasion were very satisfactory. The time limit seemed too short and a great deal of confusion might have been avoided if intending speakers had known the conditions by announcement on the bills. The time of starting was too late I think. I have no desire to blame the Chairman. His conduct under very trying circum- stances was admirable, in fact it was only his firmness, which prevented the peace party making war, and storm- ing the platform in the name of Christianity. Peace parties if you'll notice are very pugnacious if you don't give them all their own way. The notable featuie of the debate was of course the irrelevancy of about nine-tenths of what was said, and this is one of the evils which a debating society'should remedy. Mr. Harry Roberts condensed all the common sense in a few senteacez, in my opinion, but if he was responsible for. the, time limit he might have remembered that condensation is a gift which only a few possess. As I have had some experience of Parliamentary Debating Societies, kindly allow me to suggest what in any opinion are the essentials of success. Assuming that the leaders of all political parties have agreed to join and help as far as possible, the model and copy should be the present House of Commons. It is not perfect, we know, but it is the beat we have. There should be the same number ?f Members, the same aiumbers of each of the four distinct parties, Liberal,

Conservative, Irish and Labour; the same rules of procedure, and the same programme of legislation. There is no reason why a local parliament should not be in advance of the Imperial Parliament with its measures, so long as they are on the same lines and of the same character. I don't see how any other plan or scheme can obtain general support or public confidence. There is nothing unjust about it if we allow facts, and facts only, to guide our judgment. Warr;ngton is ' represented by a Liberal who had a large majority at the last election. Therefore the position in Warrington is analagous to the position in the House of Commons. That is the dominating fact. To say that changes have taken place would be to say something we cannot prove. It is only assumption. Conservatives, who don't like being in a minority, would be perfectly at liberty to do all they could to convert the majority to their views and in the process they would perhaps learn to sympathise a little more than some of them do with Mr. Balfour. We need not go to the South of England for any scheme nor is it necessary to have private consultations with men of ability in the town. We don't want any secrecy in connection with it. Let the subject be discussed in the official organs of each party, and let the conclusions be summed up and presented in regular order by those who are authorised to do so. It will be obvious that any Parliamentary Debating Society which may be formcd on a narrow basis and in an unparliamentary manner will be short- lived. It will die of ridicule.—Yours Scc.. DEMOCRAT.

div.head: WAR OR PEACE.
div.p: WAR OR PEACE.
Captain Crosfield's Reply to a Critic. THE NATIONAL SERVICE LEAGUE DEBATE.

Your correspondent in last Saturday's issue is somewhat drastic in his comments on the National Service League debate which took place on November 18th. He complains that there was neither clear nor convincing argument. I admit there was a good deal of extraneous matter introduced, chiefly by the so-called Peace Society, but nevertheless the real issue was dealt with simply and effectively. For at the very outset Mr. Stevenson maintained that to be prepared for war was to make for war. He stated that clearly and boldly. lie would that England should begin to disarm even though other nations were loth to follow. He feared no wolf. _

The supporters of the National Service League con- demned such a doctrine in the strongest possible terms as being a direct menace to the peace of Europe. This was clearly stated during the debate. There was nothing here involved or nebulous. Yet your corres- pondent complains that our 'arguments were not clear. We maintained that if England is weak she, because of her vast treasures, becomes a tempting prey to other nations who are prepared. That of course if one nation only is prepared and the others are not, then the preparation of the one does not make for peace. But where all are prepared the cost of war becomes so great, the chance of success so uncertain, that discre- tion becomes the better part of valour—the game, to use an old but expressive motto, is not worth the candle. , Mr. Stevenson, as aforesaid, does not admit that preparation for war is the best way to prevent war. , His argument is that the best way to bring about peace is not to be in a position to fight. That is the issue between him and the National Service League. I hope this portion of the debate is now somewhat clearer to your correspondent. To proceed further. The League says: Of all the various kinds of preparation for war that one is the most to be commended which brings home the responsibility of war, its horrors and its sacrifices, to the minds of the whole people. A. citizen militia, such as the Swiss have, does this. Moreover the members of this force are civilians in the first place and only soldiers in the second. It is only some dire necessity or some noble cause which is going to make them willing to fight, for it will be either to protect their dear ones or to vanquish the tyranny of an oppressor. The analogy between the citizen soldier and the fire brigade man may not be as complete as one would desire. Analogies seldom are. Yet it is nevertheless a useful analogy and one which I have no hesitation in repeating, i.e., that the fireman because he has been taught the business of putting out fires does not therefore wish to create fires. Nay, rather he has a much greater interest than other men that there shall he no fire for 7w is the one who will have to face the scorching flames and the stifling smoke. So likewise the man who has been taught to defend not only himself but his belongings has a much greater interest than the shirker that there shall be no war because if there is it is he and not the mocker at the Saturday afternoon hero who will have to face the "pitted hail of bullets which tell not whence they were sent."

In conclusion your correspondent appeals to history. I also appeal to history. Europe has never known such peace as during the last 35 years. Yet Europe is an armed camp. She counts her soldiers by millions. She is far more thoroughly and effectively prepared for war than she was in the pre- ceding portion of last century. Here is an historical proof that preparation for war, especially when the preparation involves a whole people, makes for peace —is a prevention of war even as the house well guarded is a prevention of robbery.—Yours, etc.
GEORGE CROSFIELD

div.head: TEACHERS' SALARIES.
div.p: TEACHERS' SALARIES.
A Warrington Grievance

The annual meeting of the Warrington branch of the Natipnal Federation of Assistant Teachers was held at the Wycliffe Memorial Hall on Friday evening, Mr. J. Armstrong presiding over a fair attendance. The conference of class teachers in elementary schools was held at Leeds in September last, representatives from all parts of the country attending. Mr. Edden, who attended on behalf of the Warrington class teachers submitted an interesting report. Mr. J. MORGAN was installed as president for the ensuing year, and he said there was need for strong co-operation, in order to retain all the advantages they had secured in the past, and to press forward the just claims of class teachers, whenever and wherever occa- sion arose. One crying evil was with them still, and that was that of large classes in their elementary schools Only those who had had actual experience in school work, realized the amount of preparation and worry that the management of a large class entailed. The Board of Education would allow no teacher in a Secondary School to be responsible for more than 30 scholars. Why, then, should teachers in elementary schools be compelled to have control of classes twice (and sometimes even more) than that number ? Another problem which concerned them was that of salary. Perhaps teachers in Warrington were not the worst paid teachers in the country, neither were they the best paid, but the scale adopted by the National Union of Teachers for provincial class teachers, and that in vogue in Warrington made an interesting comparison: For Men. For Women. Mm. Max. Min. Max. Union Rate ... 90 ... 180 _Warrington .. SO ... 145 _ _ _ _

IPerhaps some of them would not be so anxious to sup- plement their earnings by taking up evening school Iwork, if they received more liberal remuneration for teaching in day schools. Then, again, further new schools were contemplated. But for positions in these new schools, no Warrington class teacher need apply, unless he or she was prepared to accept a reduction of salary. To a teacher only recently certificated that would probably make no difference, but to one who had been certificated a few years, it was a serious matter. All appointments to Council schools were considered by the managers as absolutely new appointments, so that, although a teacher might have been working in Warrington for some years, and had secured an advance each year, he would have to go back to the salary at which he commenced, if he desired an appointment in a Council school. Thus, local class teachers of any experience were practically barred from taking a posi- tion in the new local Council schools : and that, under the same general committee. Surely, in an up-to-date school, a teacher ought to do better work, and in his opinion, receive a higher salary, rather than a lower. It ought rather to be, at any rate, that a teacher employed in the borough. accepting an appointment in a Council school, should suffer no pecuniary loss. (Hear, hear.) The election of officers resulted as follows :—Presi- dent, Mr. J. Morgan (St. Barnabas' School) ; Vice- President Mr. C. Yates (St. James' School) ; Treasurer, Mr. T. Edden (Heathsicie School) ; Secretary, Mr. G. Newborn (Heathside School) ; Committee, The Misses Brookes (Fairfield School), Corney (Sacred Heart School) ; Williams (Ellesmere-street Infants), and Messrs. P. Longshaw (Hamilton-street School), I. Bowen (Arpley-street School) and J., Price (St. Mary's, Buttermarket.) It was with feelings of regret that the members Present heard of the resignation as secretary of Mr. S. Jeffery, he having held the office with marked ability and tact since the inauguration of the branch nearly five years ago. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to him for his services.

with flowers of lace and a sash of vieux rose. She

wore a brown velvet hat trimmed with a large pink feather. The bridesmaids' bouquets were composed of roses. Miss Schilizzi acted as " koumpara "and wore blue nattier liberty dress, embroidered in the same shade of silk, long fur coat of vizon and velvet hat, sable colour, lined with blue nattier and trimmed with feathers to match. brother of the bridegroom, discharged the duties of best man. Two sons of the Baron and Baroness de Morpurgo acted as torch bearers, their duty being to hold up large lighted candles during the whole of the service.

lAfter the ceremony a reception was held at the ; Hotel Continental, the newly married couple being the recipients of hearty congratulations. Among the 1 invited guests were : - Mr. and Mrs. Delannis (Greek Ambassador), Mr. and Mrs. Schilizzi, Baron and ; Baroness de Morpurgo, Mme. and Mlle Parodi, Mons. and MM. The bride's travelling dress was of tailormade grey tweed trimmed with brown, the sealskin hat to match being trimmed with violets and camellias.

div.head: WEDDING of Mr. A. iH. CROSFIELD M.P.
div.p: WEDDING of Mr. A. iH. CROSFIELD M.P.

At the British Consulate in Paris on Saturday Mr A. P. Inglis, M.V.0., celebrated a marriage betrreen Mr. Arthur H. Crosfield, M.P. for Warrington, son of the late Mr. John Crosfield, of Walton Lea, near Warrington, and Domini, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. E. M. Elliadi, of Southport and Smyrna. It is interesting to note that Mrs. Elliadi is connected with the old

family of Homer, the original stock of the great Greek poet of that name. The Civil Marriage was followed on Monday by two religious ceremonies: the fitst at the English Church in the Rue d'Agnessau, the Right Rev. Bishop Ormsby, D.D., officiating; the second service being at the Greek Church in the same after- noon, when the elaborate Orthodox marriage rites were celebrated by the Archimandrite, M.G. Vassilakis assisted by the Deacon M. E. Petzalis. There was a large congregaticn consisting of relatives and friends of the bride and bridegrcom. The Greek Church is a very beautiful edifice, the walls being adorned with valuable paintings. On Monday it looked particularly striking, decorations of choice flowers having been introduced specially for the occasion. The ceremony lasted about an hour, , and was characterised by that ornate ritual which is , associated with the services of the Orthodox Church The priests wore gorgeous vestments of gold and lace and there was lovely singing by a choir. Each rite had to be celebrated three times to symbolise the Holy Trinity. The whole of the service was in Greek, and a singular fact—to the English mind—was that neither the bride nor the bridegroom had to speak a word. One rather quaint and pleasing ceremony was the placing of a crown of orange blossom on the heads of the bride and bridegroom alternately. The bride, who was given away by her father, looked very charming in an ivory liberty satin directoire skirt, quite simple, with three big pleats, and bodice entirely trimmed with point d'applique lace. She carried a bouquet of choice roses. There were two bridesmaids, Miss D. Elliadi, sister of the bride, who was attired in pink mousseline de soie trimmed with garland of roses in liberty satin, and pink tulle hat lined with mordere velvet ; and Miss

div.head: LIBERAL PARTY'S GIFT.
div.p: THE LIBERAL PARTY'S GIFT.

Owing to the short notice which was given of Mr. Crdsfield's approaching wedding there has not been time for organising an adequate presentation from the Liberal Party in Warrington. Steps are now being taken to secure subscriptions from all sections of the party in order to make such a gift to Mr. Crosfield as will express in a tangible form the appreciation in which he is held by a host of supporters.

div.head: LIBERAL ASSOCIATION'S MESSAGE.
div.p: LIBERAL ASSOCIATION'S MESSAGE.

On Monday the following message was wired to Mr. Crosfield at the Hotel Continental, Paris : "Warrington Liberal Association wishes you health, happiness, long life, and a continued reign at Westminster on behalf of our ancient borough.—J, T. LOCKER, hon. secretary."

div.head: JUNIOR LIBERALS' CONGRATULATIONS.
div.p: JUNIOR LIBERALS' CONGRATULATIONS.

At the meeting of the Junior Liberal Association on Monday evening Mr. H. W. Guest,one of the secretaries announced that during the day he had sent a congratu- latory telegram to Mr. Crosfleld, in the name of the Association. On the proposition of Mr. Guest, seconded by Mr. Ford, the meeting formally passed a resolution expressing their heartiest good wishes to Mr. Crosfield and his bride.

div.head: PRESENT FROM EUPLOYEES OF MESSRS. JOSEPH CROSFIELD & SONS LTD.
div.p: THE PRESENT FROM EUPLOYEES OF MESSRS. JOSEPH CROSFIELD & SONS LTD.
PRESENT FROM THE WORKS.

The nappy event was duly celebrated at the works of Messrs. J. Crusfield and Sons, Ltd.,where Mrs. Crosfield is held in the highest este.em and regard. Flags fluttered gaily in the breeze, and during the day a merry peal was rung on tubular bells, which had been placed on the roof of the works. It was natural that the employees should wish to express their good wishes in tangible form, and the result is that Mr. Crosfleld has been the recipient of an exceedingly beautiful present from the whole of the staff and wor'ipeople. It takes the form of a solid silver fruit and flower epergne, of elegant and Llaborate design, on an ebony plinth, and two solid

silver candelabra to match. The epergne bears the following inscription :—" Presented to A. H. Croatia's', Esq., M.P., by the commercial managers, travellers,and general office staff of Joseph Crosfleld and Sons, Ltd., Warrington, on the occasion of his marriage, 2nd December, 1907." Each candelabra is inscribed as follows :—" Presented to A. H. Crosfield, Esq., M.P., by the technical staff, foremen and workpeople of Joseph Crosfleld and Sans, Ltd., Warrington, on the occasion of his marriage, December 2nd, 1907" Two handsomely illuminated books—one from the staff and the other from tha workmen—containing the names of the subscribers, are being prepared.

div.head: MAYOR'S GOOD WISHES.
div.p: THE MAYOR'S GOOD WISHES.

The Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) sent a congratu- latory wire to Mr. Crosfield on Monday from the Mayoress, himself, and the Corporation. On Tuesday evening he received the following acknowlsdgment from Mr. Crosfield :—" Mille remerciements. Please give our liberal greetings to everyone for kind message.—Arthur and Domini Crosfield."

div.head: POETIC CONGRATULATION.
div.p: A POETIC CONGRATULATION.

Mr. R. Storey writes :—On receiving your issue of Saturday last containing the excellent photographs of our Member and his bride, the following lines came into my mind : Long may the marriage union blend In peace and love till death doth end The bond that makes you one; And grace and goodness crown your days, God bless and guide all your ways, Then Jesus say " Well done." A WEDDING PEAL.

The bells of St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, Warrington, rang out a special wedding peal on Monday at 12 noon for half-an-hour, Mr. Croatiald being one of the donors of the fine peal of eight hells.

div.head: MR. HOWES' JOCULAR REFERENCE.
div.p: MR. HOWES' JOCULAR REFERENCE.

Mr. JOSEPH HowEs, in a spo3ch at the meeting held in the Co-operative Hall under the auspices of the Progressive Labour League on Wednesday evening, said that whether they were Liberals or Tories they could all send a cordial and warm vote of sympathy with their Member in his new undertaking. (Laughter and applause.) "He has got married more than onoe ' continued Mr. Howes—" so I suppose it is a perfect Job. (Laughter.) I was only married once myself and it has lasted right up to now. (Laughter.) In a short time after the honeymoon is over, Mr. Crosfield will return to his "love " here and we shall have an opportunity of welcoming the Member and his wife. I think it is quite time he took a wife and settled down, and we shall all be glad to see both of them." (Applause.) Mr. W. E. HARVEY, M.P., also extended his con- gratulations to Mc. Crosfleld and wished him much happiness. They could all rejoice with those who did rejoice and he could well understand that the present must be a time of rejoicing for their respected Member. Might he and his bride live long to enjoy happy com- panionship. (Applause.) Mr. J. WILLETT said he had just returned from Paris after seeing the marriage ceremonies and Mr. Crosileld wished him to thank Mr. Harvey for coming to Warring- ton and to convey his best thanks to the meeting. He (Mr. Willett) could say in all sincerity that a better man than Mr.Crosfleld they could not have to represent them. (Applause.) POPUL kR ON THE CONTINENT.

The " World " Continental supplement, under the bead" Cannes," says :—The topic of the moment in the English social and golfing world is the announced engagement of the popular captain of the Cannes Golf Club, Mr. Arthur H. Crosfleld, M.P. for Warrington, to Miss Domini Elliadi. Miss Elliadi is also a golfer, but she is a very fine lawn tennis playor,and her record as a Continental prize-winner has few equals. A naturalized Greek, her father has lived in England, where Miss Elliadi was born. The wedding will take place in Paris very soon, and the honeymoon will be passed in England. Later it is probable that the popular pair will spend some time at the Bellevue, Cannes.
For Bronchial Coughs take Woods' Great Peppermint Cure. 1/li, 2/Q.—Advt.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCH.

The twenty-fifth anniversary of the re-opening after restoration was observed on Sunday in the Parish Church of St. Lawrence, Frodsham, one of the most beautiful, dignified, and commanding edifices in the diocese. Built 800 years ago, it was restored in 1882 at a total cost of £12,000, and is as good and firm now as it was twenty-five years ago. The anthem, "I was glad" (Elvey), taken on Sunday was the one sung a quarter of a century ago at there-opening service,whilst two choirmen, Mr. Alexander Jones (tenor), and Mr. Peter Nickson (bass), had the honour and privilege of taking part in both services, having now been choristers for considerably over thirty-five years. The Rev. W. L. Paige Cox preached eloquent sermons to large con- gregations. Only three of the original Executive Committee, including the Vicar (the Rev. H. B. Blogg), are living, and one has left the parish; whilst both architects, Messrs. Bodley and Garner, have gone to their last rest. The organist of twenty-five years ago (Mr. Thomas Riley) is the vicar's warden to-day. WIDNES BLAST FURNACE EXPLOSION.

Mr. Coroner Brighouse held a resumed inquest at the Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday touching the death of Martin Cain' who died on the 15th of last monnh at the Widnes Accident Hospital, from severe burns received through an explosion of a blast furnace at Messrs. Bolton and Sons' copper works, Hutchinson-street. Mr Beard, his Majesty's Inspector, was present. Mr. Glover appeared for the firm and Mr. Thomas for the relatives.—ThomasWalker said he was departmental manager. The works had been in existence for twenty-live years, and they had never had a fatal accident before. The furnace which exploded was a blast one, a rectangular brick building braced together with steel channels. It was used for the melting of slag or ore, by means of coke and blast. In this furnace are a number of tuyeres, and one of these (produced in court), through an insufficient supply of water for cooling purposes, had burned at the end and burst. The water could be regulated by means of a valve, and it is thought that this had been turned off.— William Burgess, Charles-street, said that at a quarter to nine Cain sent for him, and asked him to have a look at a tuyere at the back, as it was not running properly. Witness were to the tap to see if the water was on,when the explosion occurred, and he was knocked down.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
THEFT AT EARLESTOWN.

James Skeecb, of Newton-le-Willows, was fined 40s. and costs, at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, for stealing a number of workmen's tools, valued at is. Gd., from the Vulcan Foundry, where be was formerly employed.

div.head: OBITUARY.
div.p: OBITUARY.

The death took place on Saturday of an old Earles- town resident at her residence, Swan-terrace, Newton Common, at the age of 81. Deceased was the widow of Mr. G. Naylor, and was the licensee of the Swan Hotel, Newton Common, for over 23 years, now in the occupa- tion of her son, Mr. John Naylor. The death took place suddenly on Saturday of Mr. J. Eckersley, Wargrave-road, storekeeper for the Sankey Sugar Company for elose upon 50 years. PRESENTATIONS TO P.C. PROCTOR.

The retirement of P.C. Proctor from the police force after 25 years has been signalised by a couple of presen- tations. On Saturday, at the Earlestown Police Station P.C. Proctor was the recipient of a very handsome marble clock from his fellow officers station9d at Earlestovvn. The clock bore the inscription on a silver tablet : " P.C. Proctor on his retirement from the Police Force, after 25 years' service, by his comrades November 30th, 1907." At the same time Mr. Kinch, Mr. Ireland and Mr. T. Fairclough, representing the residents of the town, presented P.C. Proctor with a pair of bronzes and a purse of gold.— Inspector Tunes represented the police, and spoke in eloquent terms of the constable's career since he had known him, and wished him every good wish for the future.

WAGGON-MAKERS' DINNER. The members of the Waggon Makers' Union held their annual dinner at the Viaduct Hotel on Saturday evening, about CO sitting down to the 'excellent repast served by Mr. and Mrs. Tunstall. A concert was afterwards held and songs were given by members of the society, each item being well received. Mr. McLeary, chairman, spoke of the work being done in the district by this society.—Bro. Schofield also spoke on the same subject.—Mr. Lancaster, of Wigan, general s2cretary, in his address said he was pleased to say the society was in a better condition financially and other- wise to-day than it had ever been before. (Cheers.) —A vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman and General Senretary, which both gentlemen acknowledged. The meeting closed with the singing of the National Anthem. Mr. J. Hales was the accompanist.

NEWTON URBAN COUNCIL. The monthly Council meeting was held in the Council Chamber, at the Earlestown Town Hall, on Monday evening. Mr. T. Ormand presided, and these were also present :—Dr. Patterson, and Messrs. W. Thompson, C, B. F. Borron, W. Collingwood, F. Harwood, A. Tunstall M. Seton, E. L. Bent, T. Ritchie, B. T. Evans, G. F Clarke, J. Naylor, C. Cole (clerk), J. Bowes (surveyor) and R. T. Surtees (water engineer).—At a meeting of the Sanitary Committee it was resolved that the Medical Officer of Health be asked to report upon the outbreak of diphtheria in Wargrave Ward, and as to the steps taken to stamp out the disease. At a meeting of the same committee it was resolved that the Council be recommended to give notice that at the January Council meeting Mr. Henry Ashcroft be re-appointed Inspector of Nuisances for the district for one year from the 25th January next at the same salary as heretofore. The minutes were approved.—The Council resolved "That Councillor Bent having been absent from meetings of the Council for more than six months consecutively and having explained that such absence arose through his illness and other unavoidable causes, the Council approve of such reasons for his non-attendance in pursuance of Section 46 (b) of the Local Government Act, 1894." At a meeting of the Higher Education and Technical Instruction Committee, on November 18tb, the Clerk reported that he had written to the Clerk of the County Council with reference to the recent communication from the Local Government Board on the subject of an amendeo agreement, and read his reply thereto, in which he stated that he was awaiting a reply from the Local Government Board aa to form the agreement between the County Council and the several local authorities should take.

MR. SEDDON, M.P., AND LABOUR REPRESENTATION. Mr. J. A. Seddon,. M.P. presided at a meeting of railway workers and sympathisers in the Garston Co-operative Hall, on Sunday afternoon, and, referring to the railway settlement, desired to strike a note of warning. He was informed that a process was already goin,, on of weeding out those men who had been in the forefront of the battle. The whole funds of the Amalgamated Society should be expended in defending such men against the tyranny of the companies. He appealed for general support for the organisation, declaring that the great lesson they had to learn was solidarity of the whole workers of the country. When one part of the body suffered, all suffered, and their first duty was to raise the bottom dog. He made bold to say that through politics they could use the Parliamentary machine so that every individual who contributed either by brain or muscle to the community should have a fair share of the wealth produced. The great majority were defrauded out of their fair return for the labour they gave. (Hear, hear.) Except in the very highly- skilled and efficiently-organised industries the great bulk of the workmen were working for a bare subsist- ence for the moment, and hardly any could look to the future with equanimity. Machinery, instead of being a blessing, had been a positive curse to the workers, and the Liberal and Conservative parties looked on helpless Only by an efficient Labour representation in Parlia, ment could the problems of industry and economic_ be settled with satisfaction to the workers. (Applause.s

industrous workman, and they very much regretted his loss.—The Coroner said the most practical sympathy the company could show would be to award the widow something.—Mr. Bland thought the company would be perfectly just, as they always were in those cases.—The Coroner said in a case of that sort where there was some evidence, but not sufficient, the company ought to be as generous as they could.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
MARRIED WOMEN TEACEi ERS TO GO.

The St. Helens Education Committee have directed all the managers of the elementary schools of the borough that the services of all married women employed as teachers,otherwise than as supply teachers, shall be dispensed with before July 31st, 1909.
SUDDEN DEATH OF A k. HELENS TRADESMAN.

Great sympathy is expressed in St. Helens with the family of Mr. James Hulme, whose eldest son, Mr. Ernest Hulme, died on Sunday evening suddenly. Mr. Hulme, junior, was twenty-four years of a2e. and was married. He WAS associated with his father in the boot business in Bridge-street, and was at work until Satur- day night. He was taken ill en Sunday, and suddenly collapsed. Deceased was a prominent member of the Wesleyan congregation. DOG SHOW AT ST. HELENS.

The South Lancashire Canine Association held an open show at St. Helens on Saturday, when the exhibits were very numerous and the show of dogs quite the finest ever seen in the town. The work of the judges was considerably interfered with by the thick fog, which rendered it necessary to illuminate the judging marquee. Mr. J. Mackay (chairman), Mr. J. Swinburne (hon. secretary) and all the other officers worked hard for the success of the show, and did all in their power to accommodate the exhibitors, whose travelling arrangements were rendered difficult by the chaos on the railvcay. Mr. A. R. Hughes judged the great danes. Mr. R. Walling the collies and bobtails, Mr. 0. J. Burgess the retrievers and spaniels, Mr. J. W. Mansell the bull dogs, Mr. H. Stafford the Airedale and Irish terriers, and Mr. P. Howard the fox terriers. LABOURER'S TERRIBLE DEATH.

Alexander Ross, labourer, forty-one, of 105, College street, St. Helens, met with a shocking death at Messrs Pilkington's plate-glass works, Cowley Hill, on Saturday afternoon. He was enzaged at the extension grinding shed, along with four other men, in wheeling iron bars from a staging outside the shed to one inside, and there piling them in stacks. He had just wheeled a full barrow on to the inside staging when the staging suddenly collapsed, and deceased was precipitated into a hole ten feet below, the barrow and iron bars falling upon him, Dr. Bailey was at once sent for, and he ordered the unfortunate man's removal to the St. Helens Hospital, where it was found that he had received terrible injuries, from which he shortly after- wards succumbed.

div.head: SPIRITUALIST SALE OF WORK.
div.p: SPIRITUALIST SALE OF WORK.
. _ Interesting Speech by Mrs. C. E. Parker.

A sale of work in aid of the funds of the Warrington Spiritualist Society, commenced at the Druids Hall on Wednesday afternoon and continued on Thursday. The ladies had worked hard to promote the success of the event, and there was a large display of useful and fancy wares. The following is a list of the stallholders : LYCEUM STALL :—Miss Ashurst and Miss Dark. FANCY STALLS :—Mrs. Hardman, Mrs. Naylor, Mrs. L. Davies, Mrs. Simpson, Mrs. Roberts. REFRESHMENT STALL :—Mrs. Bailey. BORDERLAND (Wednesday) :—Mrs. Crompton and Miss Chadderton. (Thursday) : Miss Chadderton and Mrs. Hazlehurst. WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

The sale was opened on Wednesday by Mrs. Parker The chair was occupied by Mr. W. E. Stout (president of the Society), and Mr. C. E. Parker was also on the platform. The CHAIRMAN said the object of that two days sale of work was to provide the Society with a room, as the hall they now occupied had to be demolished for street improvement. They found that their first room, which was in Academy-street was too small so they went to a room in Besysey-street. They afterwards went to the present room and now they had to move from there. They had £4O in the bank. (Applause.) He was sure they were all pleased to see Mrs. Parker amongst them once more and he had great pleasure in asking her to declare the sale open. (Anplause.) Mrs. PARKER said : VS,nen Mr. Stout invited me to open your sale of work this afternoon, he gave as his reason, that I had manifested some interest in Spiritualism. As a matter of fact, I have taken a very deep interest in the subject for many years and there- fore responded gladly to your kind invitation to be present to-day. Spiritualism appeals to me in many ways. First, because of its saneness, its reasonableneas, because it shows the naturalness of the supernatural, if I may so put it ; it brings the after-life so near to the present•earth-life and helps us to realize, as nothing else does, that the after-life is not only sequential to earth-life, but an actual continuation of it, subject to the same great laws, and with no break save the laying aside of the earth vestment. It also gives one a truer sense of the relation between earth and future life. While I would not for one moment under-rate the importance of the present, we realize that it is but as a vestibule to a larger chamber, that the allotted space of earth life merely prepares us to pass on to a sphere where, in freer, ampler conditions we may continue our development through mons to come. By this realization we find the strongest incen- tives to the culture of all that is best within us, mental. moral, spiritual, and to true, noble, and unselfish living' And I would wish to see that in so far as I have read and investigated this and kindred subjects, not only have I found nothing which weakens the essentials of Christian faith, but much that illuminates them. I could wish that modern Christianity had more of the spiritual atmosphere which characterized the people, and the lantl in which the Christian religion had its birth. I feel that all that is truly religious in a man's character would only be quickened, elevated, and intensified by his apprehension of the unseen. The thought of the world is very much running to materialism. Nothing can so surely stem this tendency as the certainty that man has a continued existence and spiritualism is the only thing which proves this by scientific data. lam glad to be here this after- noon because I believe, that although we may not all see alike on this subject, we are at least all earnest in our quest for truth, and broad-minded enough to open our minds to it aud welcome it in whatever guise it comes. (Hear, hear,-and applause.) Mrs. Parker then declared the sale open. At this stage Miss Simpson a little girl of four, pre- sented Mrs. Parker with a beautiful bouquet. Mr. W. E. Stout then presented a book to Mr. Parker entitled,' Answers to Objections to Spiritualism." _ . • __

Mrs. bRINKWITER moved a vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Parker for their presence that afternoon and Mr. Simpson seconded. Mr. C. E. PARKER replied to the vote of thanks on behalf of his wife and himself and he said he would read the book with groat interest. THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS,

The sale was continued on Thursday when the opening ceremony was performed by Councillor Fulton-Smith. The President (Mr. W. E. STOUT), announced that he was in receipt of contributions of money and goods from members and friends in Canada and America. (Applause). Councillor FULTON-SU ITII in declaring the sale open said he thought everybody was a spiritualist. Some people laughed at the idea and thought the Spiritualists were frauds bat they were not so. (Hear, hear.) A man who was a Spiritualist was simply studying himself and making himself a betser man. (Applause.) Mr. STOUT presented Mr. Smith a copy of a book he presented to Mr. Parker and Mrs. Smith was also the recipient of a bouquet.

div.head: Beamont Council School.
div.p: Beamont Council School.

The nature study gardens at the above school which have been well laid out under the direction of Mr. Whitfield, the Corporation head gardener, are in four large sections, extending the whole length of Wilkinson-street, and contain about 1,500 square yards. Two of these sections are allotted to the boys' department, and one to each of the other two depart- ments. These gardens have been turfed, except where prevision is made for HO plots, each of which will be under the special care of a boy or a girl. It is intended to utilize these to the fullest extent. During the various seasons of the year —seed time, and growth and harvest —following a lesson given in the classroom by the teacher, the children will be taught and encouraged to practise in the garden what they have just received instruction in. The growth of the seed—the fertilization of the flower— the ripening and gathering of the seed will all be observed and recorded. These gardens will become the classrooms where those children not fortunate enough to be among the chosen will be taken for their nature study lessons. It is hoped that some scheme of awards may be instituted for the care and cultivation of the plots,and it has been suggested that the Beautiful Warrinhto.n Society might consider this matter well within their province. The ornamental gardens extend along the east frc.nt of the school for a distance of nearly two hundred yards, and will be attractively laid out with plants and flowers. It is intended also to utilize the flat roofs of the cloakrooms for roof gardens.

DEATH THROUGH A:SCRATCH 1 Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner, held an inquest at Warrington on Monday morning into the circumstances attending the death of William Eaton, aged 45, a carpenter, employed by the London and North-Western Railway, who resided at 11, Birch-street, Earlestown. Mr. Bland appeared on behalf of the Railway Company, aud Mr. Eatock, factory inspector, was also present.—lt appeared that on Thursday, November 21st, at 5.45 p.m., Eaton and another carpenter named John Oldham, 12, Lawrence-street, Earlestown, were engaged repairing a coal waggon. Both men got hold of the waggon door to lift it up and close it. As they were doing this Eaton said "I think I have sprained my arm ; I felt something go." Oldham examined the arm, but could not find anything the matter, and Eaton continued to work until 5.30, finish- ing time. On arriving home he told his wife that he had hurt his arm with the waggon door and that it was paining him very much. On examina- tion Mrs. Eaton found a swelling, about the size of an egg, on the back of the left arm above the elbow joint. , She bathed it with warm water, and the following day ' Eaton did not go to work. In the evening of November 2nd, he saw Dr. Harold Ernest Watkins, who, with his assistant, examined the arm. Eaton was ordered to bed , and was medically attended until the 256, when he was taken to the Warrington Infirmary. There he was attended by Dr. Hodgkinson, and on the 213th it was thought necessary to perform an operation. Eaton died on Thursday, November 25th.—Medical evidence showed that death was due to blood- , poisoning set up by a small scratch on the CHILD CHAIRMAN. arm. How the scratch caused it was impossible to say— The jury, after considering the case in private, returned Master Tom Sellwood, aged eight, presided at the a verdict to the effect that death was caused through the opening of a Wesleyan bazaar on Thursday at Brentford, scratch, but that there was not sufficient evidence to and made a remarkable speeca. His address was prove how the scratch bad been caused.—Mr. Bland received with applause, and when he had concluded a expressed the company's sympathy with the deceased's little suggested that he should be thanked for his "wise relatives. Eaton was regarded as an excellent and and enc9uraging remarks and dignified conduct."

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT MOORE. Address by Mr. A. J. King, M.P.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT MOORE. Address by Mr. A. J. King, M.P.

A meeting under the auspices of the Knutsferd Division Liberal Association was held on Wednesday evening in the Schoolroom, Moore to hear an address from Mr. A. J. King, M.P. Mr. Hilbert Congreve was in the chair. There was a fairly large attendance which included—Miss Bessie Dutton and Niessrs.Josiah Longland, C. Roylance, W. H. Sherburn and Mr. Joseph Smith (election agent), Letters of apology for non-attendance were read from Mr. Ziba Armitage and Mr. C. J. Holmes. The Chairman said he was very glad to see them all there that evening and to see the best gathering he had ever had the pleasure of attending in that portion of their division. They welcomed Mr. King amongst them to hear him give an account of his stewardship as their representative in the House of Commons. They could rest assured and say they were satisfied with Mr. 'Zing. (Hear, hear, and applause.) They were satisfied with him as their Member, and they were extremely grateful to him for taking such a great interest and doing his best to satisfy the electors in all parts of the division. The Chairman went on to say that the taxes had greatly decreased since the Liberal Government came into puwer. Germany wus taxing every mortal thing because they had such great military forces to maintain. There would some day be as great a crisis in Germany as there was in America. (Hear, hear.) The Government had now under consideration the Small Holdings Bill. Lord Carrington was in charge of an enormous amount of land and he was letting it out in small plots. The Government was trying the experiment of making (mule land in Scotland into forest land. Parliament also had under consideration the tiousing question. In conclusion the speaker told the audience not to be led away by false statements of the Tories. He then called upon Mr. King to give his address. (Applause.) Mr. A. J. King. M.P., who had a hearty reception said they had a good House of Commons and they had got a good leader and he thougbt be would endorse the feeling of all present when he hoped that his health might be spared for a good many years to come. (Hear, hear.) Be (Mr. King) always endeavoured to do all he could to help the workingmen of his division. He hoped they would all sympathise with Mr. Lloyd George in his recent bereavement, ard also the great loss he has sustained in the death of his daughter. They had Lord Carrington at the head of the Board of Agriculture, and agriculture was part of Ilie work of the present Government. In the last tw6 yeare 120 Bills had become Acts of Parlia- ment, and during the last two years of the Conservative Government that Government had only passed 59 Acts. The present Government had already passed six Acts for the benefit of farmers. They had passed a good Bill in the Butter and Margarine Bill, which would stop people from putting on their margarine "Milk Blended Butter" when there was as much as 15 par cent. of water in it. There was another Act which enabled the tenant to claim compensation for damage done by wind and gale. Another one was to the effect that if a landlord would not repair property the tenant could have it repaired and when he left be could claim compensation. (Applause.) In referring to the Small Holdings' Act he said that Lord Carrington was letting out all the land ho was in charge of for small holdings as Mr. Congreve had said. It would make the country better off as they would got more money by letting land in several small plots than if they let a very large portion to one man. (Hear, hear.) The question of finance was a very important one especially with regard to the Army and Navy and in his maiden speech on entering the House of Commons he dealt with that very point. (Applause.) The expenditure on the Army and Navy for two years was something like nine millions less than it was before the election. As the last election they had a great majority and he thought the next election would mean a greater majority for the Liberals. (Hear, hear.) But a great deal remains to be done. A part of what remained to be done concerned the Education Question, and he was looking forward to a settlement. (Applause.) The Licensing Question would also be a very big job. They were all enthusiastic in their desire to reduce the curse of imtemperance. They were all hoping that children would not be allowed to enter public-houses, for if children were allowed to go into public-houses they would be tempted and when they get older would very likely fall victims of drink. (Applause.) A vote of thanks to Mr. King was carried enthu- siasticall 7 on the proposition of Mr. Longland,seconded by Mr. Sberburn.
-A votnof thanks Tros also accorded to the Chairman on the motion of Mr. King, seconded by Mr.C. Roylance and supported by Miss Bessie Dutton.

Al* , PADGATE; WESLEY GUILD.—On Monday evening at the meeting of the Guild members held in the Wesley's.] School- room, Padgate, Mips Jessie Ward gave a paper on "Three phases of Man" in regard to his relation with nature and his God. The essayist dealt with her subject in a most able and edifying manner, her practical refer- lances boing both touching and inspiring. Altogether the paper was of an educative and instructive character I and consequently the members spent a profitable and I enjoyable evening. FIRE ON A LINER. A fire occurred on Thursday afterooon in the forepeak of the White Star liner Afric, which is loading in Canada Dock, Liverpool, for Australia. The fire brigade turned out, but some time elapsed before the seat of the outbmak could be reached, owing to the dense smoke which was given off, and the fire WAS not overcome until considerable damage hid been done to the cargo.
